To the Reader, greetings.

You are to be advised, candid reader, that of the letters R. and S. in this work, placed sometimes over numbers, sometimes over characters, sometimes over words, either superscribed on the page or added in the margin, the former is the mark of rubric, or red color, while the latter is the mark of ink, or black color. Moreover you will observe this too: the individual titles of the individual chapters are likewise to be depicted and adorned in rubric. You may seek the significance of this matter from the Key prefixed to the work. Farewell.

Here begins the first book of the Steganographia of Johannes Trithemius, abbot of Sponheim, of the Order of Saint Benedict, of the diocese of Mainz, addressed to the most serene prince, Lord Philip, Count Palatine of the Rhine, Duke of Bavaria, and prince elector of the Holy Empire, etc.

It is the opinion of the most learned that the most ancient sages, whom in Greek speech we call philosophers, if they had discovered any secrets either of nature or of art, concealed them by various modes and figures, lest they come to the knowledge of wicked men. That Moses too, the most famous leader of the Israelite people, in his description of the creation of Heaven and Earth covered over the ineffable secrets of mysteries with simple words, all the more learned among the Jews confirm. Saint Jerome also, most learned among our own, affirms that almost as many mysteries lie hidden in the Apocalypse of John as there are words. Besides, I pass over the sages of the Greeks, held in no small esteem among their own people, and our own most learned philosophers and poets, who, devoting their effort to writing fables, [unclear] one thing to the unlearned, and another to learned men

Hos ego Sapien- tiae studiosissimos amatores etsi propter ingenij tarditatem perfecite imitari nequeo: admirari tamen, & qua possum sedulitate legere nō omitto. Quia cum illos magna prae caeteris hominibus proprio studio excogitasse considero, meipsum quadam violentia confricans, vt in- calescam, ad aliqualem vel cum nouißimis imitationem preceden- tium impello. Nec me penitus, vt reor, fesellit opinio; quicquę qui et multa, quae prius nesciueram, per continuum legendi studium didici: &amp; cogitationibus meis ad inuestandum secretiora et amp; prorfus arca- na caeteris aditum referauit. Nam etsi non sum tantae vel eruditionis vel industriae, vt me illum antiquorum sapientum mysteria occultũ di- modū apprehẽdisse ex omni parte aussim profiteri: modos tamē quos- dam et amp; multos et amp; varios, non penitus (vt mihi videtur) contemnẽ- dos reperi, quibus mentis meae secretissimam intentionem alteri hanc artem scientiae, quam latiffime voluero, secure et amp; absque illusione, suspi- cione, vel deprehensione cuiuscunque per apertos vel nuntios vel literas possum intimare. Philippi, Comitis Palatini Rhe- ni, Ducis q; Bauariae, ac Sacri Romani Imperij Principis Electoris semper inuitissimi, Philosophorũ omnium sapiẽtissimi Mecoenatis, quo nullus mihi dignior visus est, cui hoc magnū secretum reueletur, litteris comendaui, &amp; non sine maximis laboribus insubiectum volumen coportaui. Ne aüt hoc magnū secretū in aures vulgarium imperitorū aut prauorum hominū perueniat officij mei rationem existimauit non vltima, ita illud, quoniã mysteria docet intelligere nesciẽtẽ, mysterijs obuoluere, vt nemo futurus fit: ex imperitorū numero, nemorisi stu- diosissimus, ꝙ huius scientiae arcanū sua poßit virtute perfecite et amp; ad intentionē nostram penetrare ad plenum, nisi per receptionem à do- cente, [illegible]

Preface.

They handed them down, in a sequence of narration, by sagacious invention. Although, because of the dullness of my talent, I cannot perfectly imitate these most devoted lovers of wisdom, nevertheless I do not cease to admire them and to read them with whatever diligence I can. For when I consider that they, by their own study, devised great things beyond other men, I rub myself, as it were, with a certain force, so that I may grow warm, and I impel myself toward some imitation, even among the least, of those who have gone before.

Nor, as I think, has this opinion wholly deceived me; since through the continual pursuit of reading I have learned many things which I had not known before, and it has opened to my thoughts an approach to investigating matters more secret and altogether hidden from others. For although I am not of such learning or industry that I would dare profess that I have in every respect grasped the hidden method of the mysteries of the ancient sages, nevertheless I have found certain methods, many and various, not altogether contemptible, as it seems to me, by which I can safely and without deception, suspicion, or detection by anyone, through open messengers or letters, convey to another the most secret intention of my mind in this art of knowledge as widely as I may wish.

And at the request of the Most Serene Prince, Lord Philip, Count Palatine of the Rhine, Duke of Bavaria, and Prince Elector of the Holy Roman Empire, always my most unwilling [unclear], the wisest Maecenas of all philosophers, than whom no one has seemed to me more worthy for this great secret to be revealed to him, I have committed to writing this new discovery of a most secret art, and not without the greatest labors have gathered it into the present volume. But lest this great secret come to the ears of common, unskilled, or wicked men, the reckoning of my office judged it not least important so to wrap it, since it teaches one ignorant of mysteries to understand them, in mysteries, that there will be no one from the number of the unskilled, no one except the most studious, who can by his own power perfectly penetrate the secret of this knowledge, and fully according to our intention, unless by reception from a teacher,

Nã quemadmodũ aerij spiritus boni  mali à summo Deo creati in mi- nisterium  profectũ nostrum (per quorũ intelligentiam omnia istius artis secreta reuelantur) sunt nobis sine numero infiniti  penitus incõprehensibiles: ita nec huius artis nostrae, q̃ Steganographiã se- creta

Preface.

... the letters of the world, Latin, Greek, or barbarous, free from all suspicion, by which it would present one thing openly to those ignorant of the art, and another secretly to those who knew it. Nor, if this science were published among the reprobate, would the trust between married persons, contracted by sacrament, any longer remain safe thereafter: since a wife, even if hitherto ignorant of the Latin tongue, yet now sufficiently instructed, through modest, honorable, and most holy words of any language or idiom, could understand most fully the evil and immodest mind and intention of an adulterous lover or fornicator, even while her husband carried the letters and praised them as excellent; and she could, in the same way, as broadly and copiously as she wished, most safely communicate her own desire to him in the same or other letters, in a beautiful and quite highly adorned sequence. And public trust could be endangered; all letters, documents, writings, and finally the very knowledge of men could come [unclear] (which God forbid); the whole order of the commonwealth, with the passage of time, could be disturbed in no small degree.

Nor can anyone, even if he lived as many years, ever become so learned and experienced in this science with his teacher that there would not be left infinite methods, secretly, most hiddenly, and most safely sufficient in this very art of writing, and, at the will of any experienced person, of working for all purposes, which he himself has not yet grasped with his preceptor. For just as the aerial spirits, good and evil, created by the highest God for our ministry and benefit, through whose understanding all the secrets of this art are revealed, are countless, infinite, and utterly incomprehensible to us, so too [unclear] of this art of ours, which [is called] secret Steganography...

Preface.

[un]covered secrets and hidden things and mysteries, perfectly containing things open to no mortal, however studious or learned, we call [unclear]; all the modes, ways, differences, qualities, and operations will be able to be made fully penetrable forever. For this science is a chaos of infinite depth, which no one can perfectly comprehend, because however learned and experienced you may be in this art, nevertheless you have always grasped less than that which you do not know. For this profound and most secret art has this property: that it easily renders the pupil incomparably, so to speak, more learned than the master, provided he is disposed by nature to proceed, and is studious in those things which he has received in the Cabalistic tradition.

The author's protestation or oath concerning the innocence of this art, etc.

And lest any future reader of this work, when in the course of it he has often encountered names, offices, orders, differences, properties, prayers, and any other operations of spirits, through whose intelligences all these secrets of this science are closed and opened, should believe or think me a necromancer and magician, or that I have entered into a pact with demons, or that I have used, or use, any other superstition: I have considered it necessary and opportune, by vindicating it with truth, to preserve my reputation and name from so great a stain, injury, fault, and blemish by a solemn protestation in this prologue.

Therefore I say before Almighty God, from whom absolutely nothing can be hidden, and before Jesus Christ, his only-begotten Son, who will judge the living and the dead; in truth I say, swear, and protest: all and every one of the things which I have said in this work, or am about to say, and all the properties, modes, figures, operations, receptions, formations, inventions, institutions, mutations, alterations of this science or art, and all things whatsoever which pertain to its speculation, invention, attainment, practical operation, either in part or in whole, and everything contained in this volume of ours, rest upon true, Catholic, natural principles; and all and every one of them are done with God, with a good conscience, without injury to the Christian faith, with the integrity of ecclesiastical tradition, without any superstition, without idolatry, without any explicit or implicit pact with evil spirits; without suffumigation, adoration, veneration, worship, sacrifice, or offering to demons; without any fault or sin, whether venial or mortal. And all and every one of them are done with truth, uprightness, sincerity, and purity. So that the science of this invention, besides, for good use,

PRAeFATIO. vsum, nō de deceat virum sapientē, Christianum bonum atque fidelem. Nam et amp; ego Christianus sum, &amp; monasticae conuersationi voluntarie addictus: cu- pioque non aliter viuere et amp; conuensari, quam verum deceat Christianū et amp; mo- nachum sub regulā Diui patris Benedicti professum: ipsamque fidem Catholi- cam secundum traditionem S.Romanae Ecclesiae suscepi à cunabulis, bapti- zatus in nomine Patris, &amp; Filij, &amp; Spiritus sancti, quam cum ipsa et amp; vniuersali Christianorū Ecclesia teneo, credo, &amp; quā diu vixero, cū Dei auxilio semper inuiolatā firmiter feruans, corde, ore et amp; opere tenebo, nec vnquā ab ipsa de- uiare quacunque occasione intendo. Procul ergo fit à me, aut discere aut doce- re aliquid, quod sit Christianae fidei et amp; puritati contrarium, sanctis moribus noxium aut regulari proposito quo modolibet aduersum. Deum timeo, &amp; in eius cultum iuraui, à quo nec viuis, nec (vt confido) mortuus separabor. Hanc protestationē meam non sine causa toti huic operi nostro praepo sui, propterea quod nouerim plures esse futuros: qui cum ea, quae scri- psimus, intelligere nequeant, ad iniurias cōuersi, bona et amp; sancta stu- dia nostra malis artibus aut superstitiosis admīnentionibus sint con- cessuri. His, cum futuri sint, &amp; omnibus quicunque haec nostra syn- themata sunt lecturi, attente supplicamus, vt si hanc secretam tra- ditionem nostram intellexerint, perpetuo feruent occultam, nec my- steria tam miranda transfundant in publicum. Si vero non intelle- xerint (quod multis scimus futurus) discant prius, quam repre- hendant. Enimuero temerarium se iudicem ostendit, qui priusquam causae veritatem agnouerit, profert de ea sententiam. Discite prius hanc artem, &amp; postea iudicate: quam si nequiueritis intelligere, non ipsam (quia bona est) sed obtusa ingenia vestra reprobate. Scio e- nim et amp; certus sum, neminem sanctae mentis hoc opus nostrum posse re- prehendere: nisi ipsū contingat penitus ignorare. Eos autem, quibus familiarius est sapientiam spernere, quam didicisse, nec opto nec vel- lem haec mystica nostra penetrare. CAP. CAP. I. CVIVS CLAVIS ET OPERATIO TENE- tur à spiritu principali Pamersyel, anoyr madriel per ministerium ebra sothean abrulges utrasbiel. Et nadres ormenu i tules rablion hamorphiel. Ad hos fit commissio o- mniuum cum exorcismo. HVIVS primi capituli est multum difficilis et amp; peri- culis plena operatio, propter superbiam et amp; rebelli- onem spirituum eius, qui non obediunt alicui, nisi fuerit in hac arte expertissimus. Nouitijs enim et minus in arte probatis non solum non obediunt, sed etiam si ni- mis vrgeātur, eos frequenter laedunt, &amp; varijs illusionibus offen- dunt. Maliciosi et amp; infideles sunt super omnes alios aereos spiri- tus, &amp; nulli penitus nisi maximis sacramentis cōpulsi obediunt, &amp; secretum quod eis cōmittitur saepè infideliter alijs oftendunt. Nam mox vt emissi fuerint cum literis auolāt, &amp; ad eum cui mit- tuntur, sine ordine irrumpentes, sicut populus sine duce fugiens de praelio, furiosi properant et amp; aerem suo clamore replētes saepè omnibus in Circuitu mittentis arcana manifestat. Consulimus ergò, vt nemo in hac arte operaturus illos cōpellat, nec eorum ministeria anxiè requirat. Quia proterui et amp; infideles fun: cum plures ex his quos confequenter dicemus jnuenire possit satis beneuolos, qui vltrò fese offerant ad obediētiam paratos. Si quis autem proteruiam eorum experiri omnino voluerit et amp; probare ea quae diximus effe vera, hunc modum obferandum nouerit. Preface.

[unclear] use, nothing that would not befit a wise man, a good and faithful Christian. For I too am a Christian, and voluntarily devoted to the monastic way of life; and I desire to live and conduct myself in no other way than befits a true Christian and a monk professed under the Rule of the blessed father Benedict. I received the Catholic faith itself, according to the tradition of the holy Roman Church, from the cradle, baptized in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. This faith I hold and believe together with that same universal Church of Christians; and, as long as I live, with God’s help always firmly preserving it inviolate, I shall hold it in heart, mouth, and deed, nor do I ever intend to deviate from it on any occasion whatever. Far be it from me, therefore, either to learn or to teach anything contrary to the Christian faith and its purity, harmful to holy morals, or in any way opposed to the regular profession. I fear God, and I have sworn myself to his worship; from him I shall not be separated while living, nor, as I trust, when dead.

I have placed this declaration of mine at the head of this whole work of ours not without cause, because I know that there will be many who, when they cannot understand what we have written, will turn to insults and will attribute our good and holy studies to evil arts or superstitious admonitions. To these, since they will exist, and to all who are going to read these synthemata of ours, we earnestly entreat that, if they understand this secret tradition of ours, they keep it forever hidden, and not pour such wondrous mysteries out into public. But if they do not understand it, as we know will happen to many, let them learn before they criticize. For indeed he shows himself a rash judge who, before he has known the truth of a case, pronounces sentence upon it. Learn this art first, and judge afterward; but if you cannot understand it, reject not the art itself, since it is good, but your own dull wits. For I know and am certain that no one of holy mind can criticize this work of ours unless he happens to be wholly ignorant of it. But those for whom it is more familiar to despise wisdom than to have learned it, I neither desire nor would wish to penetrate these mysteries of ours.

Chapter I.

Whose key and operation are held by the principal spirit Pamersyel, anoyr madriel, through the ministry of ebra sothean abrulges utrasbiel. And nadres ormenu i tules rablion hamorphiel. To these the commission of all is made with an exorcism.

[unclear]

The operation of this first chapter is very difficult and full of dangers, because of the pride and rebellion of its spirits, who do not obey anyone unless he is most experienced in this art. For they not only do not obey novices and those less proved in the art, but also, if they are pressed too much, they frequently harm them and offend them with various illusions. They are malicious and faithless above all other aerial spirits, and obey absolutely no one unless compelled by the greatest sacraments; and the secret entrusted to them they often faithlessly reveal to others. For as soon as they have been sent out with letters, they fly off, and, bursting in without order toward the person to whom they are sent, like a people fleeing from battle without a leader, they hasten furiously and, filling the air with their shouting, often disclose all the secrets around the sender. Therefore we advise that no one intending to operate in this art should compel them, nor anxiously seek their services. For they are insolent and faithless, since he can find many of those whom we shall mention next who are sufficiently well-disposed, and who of their own accord offer themselves ready for obedience. But if anyone should wholly wish to experience their insolence and to prove that what we have said is true, let him know that this manner must be observed. Let him prepare the paper on which he is going to write, with an invocation of the divine name, in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. Then let him write on it whatever simple and open narrative he wishes

When he has said these things, and has seen that the spirits are present to him for obedience, let him continue the work begun. But if they have not yet appeared, let him repeat the things already said so many times until they appear; or else let him cease altogether, lest, compelled too much, they harm the operator. But when you have completed the letters intended, send them with a messenger to a friend approved in the art; when he receives them, let him say this conjuration: Lamarton anoyr bulon madriel traschon ebrasothea panthenon nabruilges Camery itrasbier rubanthy nadres Calmosy ormenulan, ytules demy rabion hamorphyn. When these things have been said, he will at once understand your meaning perfectly, the spirits now of their own accord offering themselves with force and crying out, so that very often even others present can perceive the sender's secret. But observe that in all letters which you send written by this art you affix your own sign, so that the man to whom you write may know through which spirits you have operated. For if he were to operate through some spirits for understanding, and you through others for sending, they will never obey him for all eternity; rather, because of the improper operation, they would both harm him and by no means reveal your secret. For all the spirits whom we use in this art guard only the ranks and offices committed to them; in no way do they interfere with others. Consider carefully all the things which we shall say in what follows. And, so that we may prove by example the things we have said, let us set out our intention in the vernacular tongue, which we shall subsequently make known to a friend in the aforesaid manner.

Let this be the secret intention of the mind of Roth, some prince, which he wishes his absent vassal to know.

Dear faithful one, it is our will, for honest cause, to make war on those of Strasbourg and to fall upon them with all our force next Wednesday after Vitus and Modestus. Therefore it is our earnest desire of you, since you are bound to us by oath and vow and obliged to faithful services: that on that same day you should appear well equipped, according to your ability, about four after midday, by Stauffenburg in the forest [Here the letters were placed thus]; you would find further instruction there, should follow it, and should not fail to come. We shall recognize this graciously toward you, and keep this plan of ours with you in high secrecy, etc.

For making this secret known to Roth's vassal, with the fuller intention of the sender, let it be written thus or in another way:

Book One. For Knowing the Places, Names, Signs, and Assigned Marks of the Spirits.

But since it is necessary for everyone working in this science to know the places, names, and signs of the principal spirits, lest through ignorance he call from the north one who is dwelling in the south, which would not only hinder his purpose but could also injure the operator, I shall therefore set before you, in a circle, the regions in which the principal spirits dwell, with their names and signs.

Here I wish you to understand by east not where the sun rises on any given day, but that place in which it was created at the beginning, which we call the equinoctial. For unless you observe this consideration most diligently, you will not be able to make progress in this art. But now I shall also teach you the [sequence?] of this table, so that from one spirit you may understand all. Let us therefore take Malgaras as an example, through whom the operation of this art is carried out in the ninth chapter of this present first book. He is western; his sign is this: ⋒. He has under him thirty who preside over the day, and they have great command for putting to flight the spirits of darkness. Subject to these are another thirty, who preside over the night and dwell always in darkness; nor do they come to the light except by the command of their princes, to whom they are subject at all times. And these in turn have under them, as guardians and ministers subject to them by full right, sometimes thirty, sometimes twenty, sometimes ten, and sometimes all; they go forth together with all at the command of their principals, and in [unclear] order. Thus, as many of their number as have been summoned by the operator, at the command of the great virtues, from the second or third order, so many servants and guardians also come with them to the principal, who is Malgaras. Again, under these are others, as messengers and doorkeepers, without a fixed number, who often assemble mingled with them. We do not possess the names of all these spirits. But those which it is necessary for the operator to know we shall set forth in each chapter. And note that all these spirits are, each with his principal emperor, in the quarter of the world assigned to him, as is clear in the table.

Book One. Chapter II. Whose prince is called Padiel. Subsolanus, having under him 10,000 daytime ministers, 200,000 nighttime ones, and many other subservitors, whose number is uncertain.

Since, as we said in the preceding chapter, Pamersiel with his aforesaid spirits is implacable and unfaithful, and does not obey indiscriminately all who desire to work in this art, but scarcely even the most experienced in it, we wish in this present chapter to make the art safer, and to demonstrate the manner of working in it through better spirits, who are benevolent, prompt, and cheerful in obeying the one who calls; who, when called in the proper manner and at the proper time, come without delay, and faithfully carry out without any deceit whatever what has been entrusted to them. Now the first principal emperor and presiding spirit of this operation is called Padiel, by the name Subsolanus, in an orbicular mansion, which is the first mansion after the east. He has under him ten thousand who preside over the day and over all daytime operations of this art; they command and bring out the nocturnal spirits lurking in darkness, who number two hundred thousand. All flee light and day, except one who is a messenger to the presiding spirits. All are good and benevolent, and they do not harm the operator unless he is malicious, or less skilled in the art. It is not necessary to call them all together, but a few suffice, and sometimes one can satisfy the operator, whether the operation is nocturnal or diurnal. For since they are

3 Of the Steganography

Let them be kindly disposed, quiet, and calm; they are more often solitary wanderers than noisy in a crowd. Therefore, when you wish to operate through them, and through them to make known the secret of your mind to someone, however absent he may be, do this. Write on paper previously prepared in the proper manner, as you know, whatever account you wish, and in whatever language, since it makes no difference: for he will perceive your mind not from the paper, but from the Spirits. While writing it, turn toward the east; when it is completed, say this conjuration: Padiel aporsy mesarpon omeuas peludyn malpreaxo. Condusen, vlearo thersephi bayl merphon, paroys gebuly mailthomyon ilthear tamarson acrimyon peatha Casmy Chertiel, medony reabdo, lasonti iaciel mal arti bulomeon abry pathulmon theoma parhormyn. When you have completed these words, you will see two, or at least one, of the Spirits very peacefully present and ready to obey your will. And to him you will entrust your secret, and he will faithfully carry it to the place you have commanded.

But when the letters come by messenger to the one to whom they are sent, if he is alone, well; if he is with others, let him withdraw apart if he can, or, if he cannot, let him turn toward the east and say this conjuration in silence: Padiel ariel vanerhon chio thatson phymarto merphon amprisco ledabarym, elsophroy mesarpon ameorsy, paneryn atle pachumgk thearan vtrul vt solubito beslonty las gomadyn triamy mefarnothy. When these words have been duly spoken, immediately the Spirit sent will appear, to reveal it without deceit and without any danger. No one malicious and wicked will easily be able to operate in this art; but the better and purer anyone is, the more willingly and with greater cheerfulness the Spirits obey him. And the more each person conceals this knowledge, the more easily he will operate. And note that this Padiel with his Spirits is appointed to announce secret advisories for the correction of evildoers, imprisonment, and punishment, as we have shown in the example set below.

FIRST BOOK.

THE SECRET OF THE INTENTION, WHICH [unclear] is entrusted not to letters, but to spirits of the second dwelling.

[unclear]

Someone has been denounced to the prince, against whom some crime of lèse-majesté, or any other crime, is alleged. He wishes him to be punished by his official, from whom he is far separated. But he does not wish to write this very thing to him, lest, if the letters are disclosed by any chance, the accused man be warned and flee, or resist after joining to himself the forces of his friends, or contrive some hostile act against the prince or the laws of the country. He writes this or any other narrative whatever to his prefect, one which he need not fear being read by everyone; but the secret he entrusts to a spirit, in the manner we have described above, which will faithfully tell his secret to the man to whom it is sent, who has first been instructed in this art.

Sincere charity. I send you a prayer, for the devotion of penitents, rather beautifully composed and brief, which the whole goodwill of my mind toward you did not wish to possess alone; and it is as follows. Deliver us, Jesus Christ, eternal Savior of all good things, and forgive the offenses of sinners, and hear our groans, calming the storms of vices and renewing the oldness of conscience; lead us back to eternal paradise. Good Jesus, forgive us our sins as we beseech you, since we have grievously offended and have often fallen back. Sweetest Savior, heal our weaknesses, we pray. Be kind to those who pray to you, most dutiful Jesus, and hear us, your servants, as we supplicate you. We are human beings, wretchedly entangled in continual miseries and sunk in the greatest storms. Rescue us, most victorious comforter of the afflicted, since our life, continually buried in frailty, is corrupted. Have mercy at last, most merciful Jesus, Savior; look upon the humility of those who love you, and do not permit us, exiles, to be drowned in the mire and foulness of vices, in the love of the world. Until now we have lain sluggish, and, bound by vices, we have made little account of our salvation and have been scarcely mindful of the coming judgment. Most kind Creator, be propitious to your servants, and save those weeping ones whom the most wretched vanity of the world has deceived. Alas, we have all neglected the way of Truth; but deliver us, fixed in the mire and exiles as we are, since you are our Savior, Jesus, who despise no one. You are the unfailing joy and everlasting happiness of the saints, our hope, the glory of Christians, the light of angels, the rewarder of undefeated martyrs, the crown of virgins, the honor of widows. Good Jesus, hear us, humble [unclear].

The First Book. Chapter III. Whose prince [is] Camuel, having under him 10 spirits presiding over the daytime operations and 10 likewise over the nocturnal, with as many under-servants, whose office is to announce the coming of the one who sends.

The first and supreme of all the spirits of the third mansion, toward the south-east, is called Camuel, very benevolent and prompt to send his substitutes to him who operates in this science according to the due form. He has indeed few ministers, but all good, willing, and faithful—namely ten who preside over the day and as many who preside over the night—who are always sent in pairs to the operator from either order; since those who preside over the day neither flee the darkness, nor those who preside over the night the light. Always, where necessity demands, in every commission of the operator the one is helped by the other; and when they appear visibly, then one is seen in a beautiful habit of mixed color, and the other is wont to stand by in the form of a bright splendor. Often, however, they appear by a sensible effect only, and are not seen, except when it has so pleased the operator. This Camuel, with his ministers and under-servants, has the authority and power of announcing to an absent friend the state, will, condition, way, journeys, coming, and departure of the sender, whenever he himself who operates in this art shall wish. When, therefore, you wish, and operate according to your will, through the angels of this mansion, it behooves you to know first of all who are the ten angels of Camuel who preside over the day, and how many substitutes each of them has, and likewise so of the nocturnal [ones]; which, that you may know perfectly, you will consider the present table.

with their own subordinates as well. The last, however, as you see, have no substitute, since 0, as you know, signifies absolutely nothing in number. Therefore, when you wish to work through these angels, prepare your paper, as is customary; and, turned toward the Eurus, write whatever narrative you wish, in whatever language you wish, which need not be concealed. When it has been completed, read the following conjuration silently: Camuel aperoys, melym meuomanial, casmoyn cralty busaco aeli lumar photirion theor besamys, aneal Cabelonyr thiamo vesonthy. When this conjuration has been completed in silence, give your commission to the spirits who are present, as you know; send them forth, doing everything in silence and without commotion, if it can be done. Afterwards give the letters, to be carried through, to whatever messenger you wish, open, so that he may go freely, because the spirits will not neglect their duty, whether the messenger comes quickly or late; of this let there be no doubt for you, for they are faithful. But you must know which spirit from those named above you wish to send, so that in the conjuration you express his name immediately after the principal one; this applies in all operations in which the names of the angels to be sent are set down in the chapter itself. But now let us set down an example of what we have said concerning those things that pertain to the office of Camuel and of his subject spirits.

Roth.

Let This Be The Most Secret Intention Of My Mind, which I wish an absent person to know through the aforesaid spirits. When I am situated at Rome, I understand from the most secret counsel of the supreme pontiff that he wishes to transfer the Roman Empire itself to the Franks. I desire to dare [unclear] the princes of Germany: by messengers I cannot, since I do not trust them; by letters I cannot, because in all the cities of Italy there are men appointed at the gates who examine passers-by most exactly. Therefore I write one devout prayer, which I send open by a messenger, along with other familiar letters closed, to the same princes. I constrain the spirits of the third mansion and command them to follow the letters to be sent. And when they have been summoned by the recipient, they are not to fail to reveal to him my secret intention, which I did not dare entrust to letters. They come, they go, they obey. We all die, because we have all contracted the hereditary right [unclear] of original guilt; and no one lives who is not going to die.

Chapter IV. Whose prince, Aseliel, dwells toward the east-south, having under him forty principal substitutes with their servants; they preside over those matters that pertain to love.

The fourth mansion from the East, in the east-south, is held by the great prince Aseliel with his spirits, of whom ten preside over operations in this art by day, twenty by night. The office of the power of all these is to announce those things that pertain to the love of women.

These thirty, moreover, as princes, have under them the same number of others, whom they send in order to their duties when they have been duly summoned by the operator. Again, under these there are still others, whose number is great. But when you wish to work in Steganography through the prince of this mansion, there is no need to call upon all the spirits subject to him; one or two is enough for you, whether the operation is nocturnal or diurnal. I shall therefore tell you the names of a few, with the number of those serving under them. From these you should always call upon one or two, whichever you wish, and you have no need of more, unless the operation is for different purposes. This is the table.

You now have, behold, sixteen princes from among the greater ones, who are under the great Afiel, of whom eight preside over the day and eight over the night. Each of them has twenty subject servants, whom they send to their duties whenever it is necessary. All the princes are good for obeying, benevolent and most ready; but their servants are not all so, since they are sometimes proud and implacable, especially toward those whom they judge to be less perfect in the art. These sixteen princes, with their subjects, are sufficient for announcing everything to you, and there is no need for you either to know or to call upon more. But when you wish to work in Steganography through Asiel, observe, according to the things customarily prescribed in the art, the place of his mansion, which is in the east-south, and call one of the spirits named above for his proper time, whichever you wish. This is the conjuration:

Aseliel aproysy. melym, thulnear casmoyn, mauear burson, charny demorphao, Theoma asmeryn diuel, casonti yearlybasamys, ernoti chaua lorson.

When the conjurations have been completed in the usual manner, add the other things that must customarily be done in the art, and the effect of your operation will most certainly follow. Let us set down an example.

Let us imagine the secret of your mind. You have a beloved woman, in whose love you are held, and she no less; but you cannot approach or speak to her because of the watch kept by her people. At last you have found a plan by which you can possess her, but it is necessary first to advise her of it. You cannot do so yourself; you do not dare by letters, lest they come into the hands of others; nor do you decide that the matter should be entrusted to messengers or old women, lest afterward they make you known. Therefore, conceal by art for a time the matter which you trust cannot be made openly. You call the invisible ministers of the art, write letters suspected in nothing, and send them to your beloved even through those same guardians; they praise the writing and give it to your beloved to read. Recognizing the sign, she calls the hidden messenger, hears the plan, sends back her consent; you approach, enter, obtain possession.

Roth. Whose supreme prince, named Barmiel, dwells in the South, having under him 10 princes who preside over the day, and 20 who preside over the night, together with their keepers; and they are over the announcing of secrets that pertain to the surrender of fortresses.

[unclear]

The great prince of the fifth mansion in the South, toward midday, is called Barmiel. He has under his dominion 10 principal dukes who preside over the day, together with their sub-keepers, and 20 in number who preside over nocturnal operations, with their servants. These are more numerous than the diurnal ones because the operation of this mansion is performed more often by night than by day. For their office is to announce secret surrenders of fortresses and cities, especially at night. But when you wish to operate in this art through Barmiel, call one of his princes, whichever you wish: he will immediately come to you with 20 servants, because no prince of this mansion is ever accustomed to proceed alone or with fewer. Commit your secret, however, not to the servants, because they are proud and malicious, but to the prince, because he is good,

By living justly we shall attain happiness; for only the humble are to be exalted, only the rash to be condemned. If you seek happiness, hold fast eternal justice; you will obtain the highest glory. Be a most fervent zealot for truth; do not love falsehood, corrupting honesty and dissolving the moderation of the soul. Flee the vanity of the world, since it is very brief. Be a lover of Justice, supplanting no one unjustly. Cultivate the virtues, flee vices; justice [unclear] freedom; beware all insolence; always be humble. Love the Savior of our souls: he who loves him will by no means die unhappily. Despise glory that passes suddenly away; love the blessedness of the saints, not to be corrupted eternally. Carefully flee the snares of our ancient enemy, whom the humility of devotion, never to be interrupted, will conquer. Be watchful, so that you are not overcome by the heat of the flesh; defend manfully the paths of justice, and you know that the guilty man of rectitude is subject to everlasting evils. Every proud man is hateful to God: dying, he will be tortured without interruption and will never be consoled. What, finally, will the proud expect except lamentation? Therefore woe to you who are exalted, worthy of eternal punishment and reserved for everlasting darkness and horrors. O most pernicious vanity of vanities. Johannes Trithemius, abbot of Sponheim, wrote this on the Ides of March, 1500.

When you receive the letters, once Barmiel’s sign has been recognized, let him immediately turn toward the south, or as soon as he can. For no danger can arise from delay, as regards the spirit’s obedience, even if much delay has intervened. For when they call, he is accustomed always to come, whether quickly or late, even if they call after many days. This is his Conjuration, after those things have first been done which the art requires to be done.

Chapter VI.

Whose supreme prince, Gediel, dwelling in the south-southwest, has under him twenty by day, and as many by night, with their servants, who have the office of announcing those things which, foreseen, contain dangers.

Over the sixth mansion, which is in the south-southwest, presides the great prince Gediel, who has under his dominion twenty other chief dukes by day, and as many by night, with their many servants. Their office is to announce all things that pertain to warning a friend of any imminent future danger whatever, especially to princes, for the defense of country, castles, and cities; to announcing all things that profit friends, those whom we favor, for their safety; and also against enemies and any adversaries whatever. For all these things it is not necessary to summon the twenty princes, but two suffice with their servants. So that you may know them by name, I shall accordingly list some of them, namely eight for the day, eight for the night.

Black. Red. Black. Red. Black. Red. Aroan Coliel Sariel Reciel 20 20 20 Naras Raniel Sadiel Cirecas Red. Black. Red. Black. Red. Black. Sahas Mashel Agra Aglas 20 20 Assaba Bariel Anael Uriel

First, before we proceed to working, you should know that at least two spirits must always be called, with their twenty attendants, without whom they proceed nowhere, although not always do all appear visible. But there is no need to be concerned about this, provided that through their invisible ministry you obtain what you intend. Therefore when you wish to work in Steganography through their ministry, turn yourself toward the south-southwest, since all of them remain there at all times with their prince Gediel; do what you know must be done according to order. This is the Conjuration:

Roth. KEEP IN YOUR MIND SUCH A SECRET AS you do not dare to commit to writing.

I am indebted to my lord for many benefits bestowed upon me; I have secretly learned the plan of his enemies, through treacherous ambushes, to seize the castle this night. I desire to warn my prince; by letters I cannot, since a search of travelers is being made by the enemy on the road; by messengers I cannot, since I know absolutely no one to be entrusted with my dangerous matter. I shall summon a spirit, entrust the secret, and send any letters I wish, merely for form’s sake, so that the prince may know who is to be summoned from the number of the spirits, since otherwise, without letters, he would not know that a spirit has been sent by me. This one goes; he anticipates the princes and the castle.

Roth. LET THE FORM OF THE LETTERS BE THIS or another; when he has read it, let him forbid going.

The highest nobility and the highest virtue of the human race is to love God purely, to seek his glory, and to adore him with uprightness of mind. For the humility of a pure heart shall reign in heaven; patience shall exalt the mind alone of a bare man. He who fears God and is most diligent shall be established in true nobility. Love God, despise the world, flee the age of iniquity, love religion, brotherly charity, the bond of peace, and the unity of those who live rightly. Christ admonishes in the Gospel that we ought not to be anxious about superfluous human cares. “Having,” says the holy Apostle, “only what is necessary, let us be content.” Let us therefore have the love of God and zeal for justice, since truly solid riches are purity of soul, simplicity of heart, disregard of earthly honor, the cleansing of beauty, and the instruction of holy morals. Let us be intent upon good works, lest vices overwhelm us; let us live innocent in all uprightness, as though we were to die tomorrow. Let us love God with a most pure heart, carefully keeping [unclear] his with humility; let us mourn for sins, at all times beseeching the most pious Savior that he may forgive us our vices and pour into us his love and humility of heart. Let us defer the desires of this world and vain and false honors, diligently thinking upon our death. To live virtuously, to love one’s neighbor, to do injury to no one, to fear God, to give alms, to feed the hungry, to defend the good, to rebuke the vices of the depraved, to persist in prayers, to despise the glory of the world, and to devote oneself to readings: these are the treasures of Christians. For the vain glory of the world is about to fall suddenly, and riches too are false, which, when we shortly breathe our last, we shall leave behind unwillingly. Justice alone is our happiness. In our humility there is glorying, and the possession of riches that will remain with us for all time: the memory of death, fear of judgment, and recollection of our sins.

When my prince has received these, or any other letters containing no secret, on seeing the sign of Gediel he knows whither it is to be turned, and which spirit is to be summoned.

Chapter VII.

Whose supreme prince is Asiriel, whose dwelling is toward Africa, having under his dominion twenty dukes who preside over the day, and the same number who preside over the night; their office is to announce the plans of princes to friends.

all have many servants under them. If two leaders from the diurnal ones are called by the operator to the service of the art, they always have twenty servants serving them; the same happens also with the nocturnal ones. Therefore, if you have called only one from among the princes, especially from the nocturnal ones, he is found to have not twenty, but only ten servants. You shall not call the diurnal ones unless at least two, because they are not accustomed to come alone; from the nocturnal ones you may summon one or two, as you please. If you have called two, know that twenty servants, and if one, ten servants, are to be added in the conjuration according to custom. And so that you may know which are to be called alone and which with an associate, consider the table.

Of these spirits, who are chief among the forty, they have the office of announcing the secret counsels of princes to their subjects and friends; from the diurnal ones you have eight, and just as many from the nocturnal ones, with their many servants, who suffice for everything; nor is there need to call the others. Carefully observe that, when you call one or two princes from those named, you express in the verse the number of their servants; for they are proud, and it pleases them wonderfully to be said to preside over many retinues. Therefore, when you wish to operate through them in Steganography, turn your face to the south-west, and do diligently what you know must be done, so that you omit absolutely nothing of those things which belong to the art. The conjuration: Asiriel aphorsy Lamodyn to Carmephyn drubal asutroy Sody baruchon, viefer palormy thulnear asmeron chornemadusyn coleny busarethon duys marphelitubra nasaron fabelronty.

Book One

When these things have been completed, those who have been called will stand by there. To distinguish them, know that the princes are commonly accustomed to appear in an airy habit, that is, sapphire-colored; but the servants in white. Entrust your secret to the princes themselves, because they are faithful. All the leaders have among themselves this custom beforehand: when the operator addresses them, they immediately send away the servants; indeed, they withdraw of themselves, lest they hear the commission. When he ceases speaking to the princes, the servants are seen standing by again.

Let the secret of the prince be of such a kind that he entrusts it to no one to be conveyed.

Roth.

The counsel of a prince is great and most secret, concerning very great and difficult matters. He wishes some other prince, a friend, to know it, because he has cause; but he fears that it may come into public, with the greatest danger to himself and his people; if, however, it is entrusted to a messenger, he fears lest he betray it, or to letters, lest they be read by someone. Therefore he calls a spirit, who will not reveal the secret; he entrusts it, accomplishes it, and is secure.

He sends letters in no respect suspect, nor fearing public exposure in any respect. Roth.

Jesus Christ, unfailing light, eternal blessedness of all the saints, creator and ruler of the universe, have mercy on us. We, weak, groaning, and weeping, ask your mercy. Grant us the strength to overcome the temptations of the devil, so that, with present evils avoided, we may obtain rest. O sweetest Savior Jesus, forgive the sins of us, the servants who pray, since we desire to serve you with all our strength. Make us always have in ourselves the fervor of your love, adorned with good works. Give us the true operations of virtues, observance of justice, and inseparable love of uprightness; make us truly humble and vigorous despisers of worldly things, so that, always burning with your love, we may love nothing earthly, and esteem nothing temporal as pleasant to us. O teacher of humility, Jesus Christ, teach us to imitate your doctrine. We are, alas, entangled in many vices, bare of good works. Save us, Jesus Christ, lest we perish. O highest truth, make us alive, refuge of souls, refresh-

Vt autem in promptu habeas, quos voces ad operationem spiritus: noueris, tibi non omnes esse necessarios, sed aliquos: & ideo sufficiant tibi duodecim pro actionibus, quae fiunt in die, & totidem pro his quae fiunt in nocte, cum servitoribus eorum. We send letters for this reason to him to whom the spirit also is to be sent: because none of the princes or servants from among those spirits comes unless he is called, either to the sender or to him to whom he is to be sent. Therefore, so that you may know to whom it is sent, from what quarter of the mansion, and what spirit he ought to call, the letters are sent sealed with the sign of the prince, and written in such a way that they delight the spirit and he desires to be refreshed by their sustenance. But concerning these things we shall speak in the last chapter.

This is the Conjuration of the Spirits for the recipient.

Book One.

Chapter VIII.

Whose Supreme Prince, Maseriel, dwells toward that quarter which we call Favonius, having under him sixty chief dukes, with their many servants.

Roth.

The eighth mansion is around the west, in that place from which the wind is called Favonius; and there dwells the great prince who is called Maseriel, with an infinite multitude of dukes, princes, and attendants. From these, thirty princes have been appointed to this art, who preside over daytime operations, and just as many who preside over nighttime operations, with many servants. All these are appointed to announce and report the secrets of the human arts, of Philosophy, Magic, Necromancy, and of all marvelous and most secret operations, which are known to very few men; and in these matters they are ready and very faithful, nor do they return unless they have completed everything that had been entrusted to them. They are quiet and come without noise, as they are commanded, by themselves with many or with few, or even without attendants, at least visibly; they terrify no one except him who, not instructed in the art, has presumed to call them by the true principles of the art, which no one easily reaches without an instructor. But so that you may have at hand whom you should call for the operation of the spirit, know that not all are necessary for you, but only some; and therefore twelve are sufficient for you for actions that are done by day, and just as many for those that are done by night, with their servants.

You have, indeed, twenty-four of the thirty principal spirits of Maseriel, with seven hundred and twenty servants; of these, the first twelve preside over operations by day, and the remaining twelve over those by night. Therefore, when you wish to accomplish something in Steganography through them, turn yourself toward the west wind, and, after first performing the necessary things required by the art, call whichever one you wish from those named above, as is fitting, and he will come without delay. The conjuration: Maseriel bulan lamodyn charnoth iabrun caresathroyn afulroy beuefy Cadumyn turiel bufan Seuear; almos lycadufel ernoty panier iethar care pheory bulan thorty paron Venio Fabelronthufy. When the spirit whom you have called appears, entrust your secret to him to be carried through safely, hesitating not at all, speaking silently to him, if you are among others, as you know.

Roth. Let the secret of your mind be such. [unclear]

You have secrets in the occult sciences, philosophy, the magic of the stars, arithmetical Cabala, or any arts whatsoever, which you desire a friend, absent near or far, to know; but they are such that it is not safe to entrust them either to letters or to messengers; or certainly that he should send secrets to you, [unclear]; or even to commend a philosopher, yet so that he not know those of others. Call one or two of the above-mentioned spirits; set forth the secret; he accepts the burden, will carry it to the friend, and will report back to you what has been entrusted by him.

Roth. Write whatever prayer you wish, or any letters you like, containing nothing secret.

Almighty, everlasting God, most just rewarder of the good, who willed your Son to be a partaker of our race, that he might redeem us most wretched from devilish envy; who, by kindness alone, overflowing, took on the uncorrupted form of our [nature] from the flower of a virginal womb, the holy archangel Gabriel announcing that the Virgin, about to conceive by your most blessed Spirit, would remain a perpetual Virgin, immaculate, brighter than men, more eminent than spirits.

Steganographia

Chapter IX. The prince of which is called Malgatharas, who dwells in the west, having under him thirty dukes for daytime actions and as many for nighttime ones; their office is to announce the private secrets of friends.

[unclear]

The inhabitant of the ninth mansion, which is in the equinoctial west, is Malgaras, the greatest prince of the west. He has under him thirty dukes who preside over the day, and thirty others who preside over the night, together with their servants. The office of all these is to announce to friends the private secrets and hidden matters of friends. The dukes are good and very ready to obey the one who calls them, especially the daytime ones, since they are more accustomed to associate among men. The nighttime ones, though they are good, nevertheless do not willingly associate with men, but greatly flee and detest the light, wishing to hide in darkness; for this reason they often appear like bats to the one calling them by conjuration. From all these we shall place twenty-four, with their names, in the table; twelve of them by day and as many by night are sufficient.

Book One

You now have, among the Malgaretic princes, twelve for daytime actions and as many for nighttime ones, with their six hundred forty servants. Note that Aroyz and Basiel are always solitary; Misiel, Barfas, Asper, and Deilas can be called two by two, but the rest three at a time. When you wish to have three, or two, or one, beware lest you err in their names. As the table teaches you, so act, without alteration, lest you fall into danger.

Song of Conjuration. Red.

MALGARAS ador chamefo bulueriny marefo bodyr Cadumir auiel casmyo tedy pleotyn viordi care viorba, chameron vesy thuriel vlnauy, bueue meuo chasmironty naor ernyfo, chony barmo caleuodyn barfo thubra fol. Once the conjuration has been spoken, be a strong and steadfast man: those whom you have called will at once appear to you visibly. But if those called from among the nighttime ones do not come at once, do not for that reason interrupt your work, but press them with repeated conjuration until they obey. For they are somewhat sluggish; they do not willingly come among men, as we said before.

Let there be a secret of the mind which one does not wish to entrust either to a person or to letters.

In matters that pertain to household affairs, money, a deposit, a loan, trust, or any business of human intercourse, you have a secret which you desire an absent friend far away to know; but it is such that it would come under public examination with the greatest danger or loss to both parties. For that reason it must be entrusted neither to letters nor to men. Therefore, so that you may be secure and need fear no one’s awareness, you turn toward the west, call a duke, and entrust the secret: he goes and faithfully carries everything through; if anything has been entrusted for you, he brings it back.

Of the Steganography

Write whatever letters you wish, in which you need fear no one’s inspection.

Health and affection. My most beloved and most singular friend, the bearer of the present letter, a native of Roermond, very beneficent and [unclear] toward our friends, whom I ask you to receive kindly, will explain his need to you. Since he has always been bound to me by an old acquaintance, I would judge it most sweet, according to my powers, to relieve him and heap benefits upon him. And would that I could apply some consolation to his misfortunes. But since I am exhausted by heavy losses, as is clearer to you than daylight, I cannot satisfy my zeal as I would wish. But you, who abound in necessary temporal things, should show yourself open-handed to a friend, and humane, just as you have been accustomed to show yourself a patron of friends’ necessities. I ask, therefore, that you lend him, under a fixed term, two hundred florins, because he is placed in the greatest need, as he will inform you. I trust that he will restore everything in full when the term appointed for him has come. If you do this, I shall give thanks that will never die, and I shall stand by you in [more serious matters?]. Act so that we may prove in deed your sincere love toward us. I wish you to know that what you do for him is done for me; nor less will you have bound him, most grateful, to you, firmly believe it, and when the term has elapsed he will restore everything most completely. For he is accustomed to keep his promises inviolate and to show himself constant to all men. Moreover, since you rejoice to hear new reports, I would like to write something. I have reared a little dog, rightly called by a Greek name [unclear], flourishing with such learning, training, and memory of all things that to some he seems to have put off the beast and put on the man. He understands Greek and Latin words; he knows how to ask pardon for his faults. Whatever I command, he does, at my nod, with gestures; he discloses the secrets of men. If you saw him imbued with such discipline of manners, you would think him more learned than many men. Ordered to open a window, he opens it; surpassing nature by his intelligence, when forbidden he puts food away. He carries a burden placed upon him; [unclear] to be shown as my zealous defender; he loves himself, plays excellently, and does altogether unusual, incredible wonders. Farewell. Johannes Trithemius, Abbot of Saint Martin in Sponheim, wrote this on March 13, 1500.

Therefore, after the customary preliminaries have first been performed, he turns himself to the West, summons the Spirit, adjuring the invisible messenger that he become visible, and that he tell no one. The song of the Spirit.

Behold, you have, of the princes of Dorothiel, from each order—the daytime, namely, and the nocturnal—24 dukes, with the number of servants, ten thousand one hundred and sixty. And note that the operation through these is much different from the rest, as we shall say at large concerning the lord [spirit]. For one must operate in this mansion according to the 12 hours of the day and night, and always four princes preside over two hours, as much in the day as in the night: so that it is not permitted you to summon another except from the order which the hour concerns. So that, if the operation is in the first or second hour of the day, call whom you wish from the first four who preside over the day; if in the third or fourth, know that a duke is to be called from the second four. And so consequently it is to be done through all the orders and the 24 hours, as much in the day as in the night. When, however, you wish to operate in Steganography through the spirits of Dorothiel himself: the general [things] customarily premised in the art being premised, write whatever letters you wish, and, turning yourself to that quarter of the world which from the wind we commonly call Chorus [north-west], call one or more of the four who preside over the hour in which you operate. Dorothiel, cusi, feor, madylon, busar, pamersy, chearianothym, baony, Camersy, vlymeor, peatha, adial, cadumyr, reneat, thubra, Cohagier, maslon, Lodierno, sabeltrusyn. These [words] said, you will see the spirit appearing whom you called, prompt and cheerful to obey, to whom you may commit your secret securely and faithfully. Look at the preceding table.

him: you call the spirit, you entrust the secret to him; he faithfully performs everything. You will give whatever letters you wish, in which you need fear nothing.

Most Illustrious Prince, I inform Your Grace that Conrad Hummel, beneficed at the altar of St. John the Evangelist, died last night. But lest Your Grace, without deliberation, grant the said altar either to one of the unskilled or unworthy, of whom I think a great number will be present, as is usually the case, expecting the said altar, instead of reserving it for a more useful man, I beg that, although I am far too unworthy for my prayers to seem to obtain any favor in the sight of so great and noble a prince, Your Grace may deign worthily to grant the aforesaid altar to the bearer of the present letters, rejecting the less worthy. I have known him to be worthy of the best benefices, since I know him to be adorned with beauty of character, learned in every way in knowledge and letters, modest, continent, temperate, and one whose love of religion will be pleasing to Your Grace. And for the benefices bestowed he will not be ungrateful, but forever mindful. Given from Spanheim, on the day before the Ides of March, in the year of our Lord 1500. Johannes Trithemius.

When the prince, or another person to whom they are sent, skilled in the art, has received these letters of mine, or almost any others, once the sign of Dorothiel has been recognized, let him turn toward the choir, where that spirit himself dwells with his leaders and servants, doing all and each of the things that the art itself requires. Then let him silently call the spirit in a subdued voice, as he knows how:

Dorothiel onear chameron vlyfeor madufyn peony oriel nayr druse mouayr pamerson etro dumeson, dauor caho. Casmiel hayrno, fabelrunthon.

When this song has been completed, if the spirit delays in coming, let him read it again up to a third time; and without any doubt he will appear visibly and will reveal to the ear the things entrusted to him.

Cap.

Chapter XI.

Roth, whose supreme spirit is called Vsiel, dwelling toward that quarter of the world which, from the wind blowing thence, we call Subcircius; he has under him 40 leaders by day and as many by night, who are over treasure.

The eleventh mansion of the whole world is called Subcircius, namely from the wind which is accustomed to come from that region. In this quarter dwells a great prince who is called Vsiel, having under him 40 princes who preside over operations by day, and 40 who preside over those by night. Their office is to announce hidden and subterranean treasures, and everything that seems to pertain to the reckoning of treasures. From these we shall name a few, and as many as are sufficient in this place for the operations of Steganography; the rest, together with the others, we reserve to be named in their proper chapter at the end of this book. And note that the leaders of this mansion, when they are called by the operator, willingly and under compulsion obey them in all things, if the operator is such that he knows how to call them duly, or even to compel them, if they should wish to appear too slowly.

Of the forty princes of Usiel, who preside over daytime operations, you have 14, with their servants, 400 in number, and 14 who preside over nighttime operations. You see two signs set opposite one another, for testing and caution concerning the treasure, as you know, so that it cannot be found by thieves. We use them for guarding the treasure that has been found while the spirit is being sent to a friend. Therefore, when you wish to work in this business by means of spirits: if the business is very great or pertains to a prince, summon whatever dukes you wish from the order of fours; if it is your own, from the order of threes; if private and small, from the order of twos; if lowly and very slight, then let it be done at night in the order of solitaries only.

Vsiel parnothiel chameron briosy sthrubal brionear Caron sotronhi egypia odiel Chelorsy meair Chadusy notiel ornych turbelsi paneras thorthay pean adresmo boma arnotiel Chelmodyn drusar loy sodiuiel Carson, eltrae myre notiel mesraym Venea dublearsy mauecar melusyron chartulneas fabelmerusyn. After these verses have been spoken toward the north-west in silence, as time and place permit, do the other things that the art itself requires, and entrust the secret to the spirit now appearing, with the seal of the deep mystery, hesitating in nothing, since all those dukes are good and faithful.

Let us suppose that you have such a secret of the mind, to be entrusted to absolutely no one.

You have found a very great treasure in the coffers of the dead or in some other place, or you know for certain that it is secretly hidden. You alone are not able to carry it away, and yet you trust none of those dwelling nearby. You have a faithful friend, but absent far away, to whom you desire to reveal the mystery, but you trust neither letters nor messenger, lest through agitation you fall into exposure and danger, and lose the profit. Therefore you summon a spirit; he carries the message, summons the friend. He comes, helps, shares. Write the letters as you wish, in which there is absolutely nothing to be feared.

I send you an oration that I composed at the wedding of a certain friend of mine. God, creator of all things, redeemer of the human race, and savior of all, lest the human race should perish, also instituted the sacrament of marriage; for we read that he joined Eve as wife to the first man and said: INCREASE AND MULTIPLY, instituting the law for preserving humanity. Afterwards God incarnate deigned to sanctify marriages by a miracle. I shall praise those who serve God well by keeping the marital [unclear]; although I am not married, I shall nevertheless rightly praise marriages.

Indeed, if marriage were taken away, the whole human race would fail and collapse. For by the use of marriages the human race exists, although ruinous, weak, and corruptible; yet without marriages it would not endure. But act in such a way that the fruitfulness of your marriages is adorned with morals and conduct, holy, and placing a stumbling-block before no one. First of all love God, continually applying yourselves to works of mercy with justice; flee impiety, cultivate rectitude, love the good, always speak praises to God, assist the poor with alms, obey the commandments of God. Do not forsake truth; honor the ministers of God; pay tithes to the churches; receive pilgrims as guests; free the innocent; feed the hungry; obey your superiors; honorably love your neighbors, inflicting injury on absolutely no one. Cultivate the Christian religion most devoutly; abhor the vain, harmful, and superstitious customs of the gentiles. Keep the teachings of the Gospels and live according to the precepts of God. Flee the pleasures of the flesh, and show yourselves honorable and good; anxiously guard purity of mind

Munditia autem cordis continuïs humilimisque orationibus non destituatur: quoni- am oratio mentem purificat, estuãtes refrigerat, temptationes diaboli pro- cul fugat. keeping [it], do not defile [it]. Remember, I beseech you, what Christ our Lord cried out in the holy Gospel: Blessed are the pure in heart, that is, those who preserve purity of soul in a muddy body for God’s sake. Let purity of heart not be without continual and most humble prayers, since prayer purifies the mind, cools those who are burning, and drives far away the temptations of the devil. Hence the most holy Apostle Paul teaches you to persist in diligent and devout prayers, so that you may overcome harmful temptations. We join you in marriage, so that you may build up your lineage, propagated by decree of law, not so that you ought to overflow with harmful pleasures. For the pleasures of the flesh kill the soul and corrupt the noblest dignity of human substance [for] things to come. Therefore, mindful of these things, know that you are wayfarers who will return to the fatherland to which you have been called back. The present life is very brief, and the delight of the world comes most swiftly to an end. Therefore live in marriage in such a way that after death you may come to the kingdom of heaven with [exultation?]. Johannes Trithemius, Abbot of Sponheim, of the order of God’s father Benedict, issued [this] on the day before the Ides of March, in the year of the nativity of the Lord Jesus Christ 1500.

When these letters, or any others, are sent to someone, once the sign of the great Usiel has been recognized, let him act secretly as he knows from the art must be done; then let him turn toward the Subcircius and say the song: Usiel asoyr paremon cruato madufyn saueyr realdo chameron ilco paneras thurmo pean elsoty fabelrusyn iltras charson frymasto chelmodyn. When this song has been said, the spirit will show himself visibly and will report the things committed to him; if anything has been entrusted to him by that man, he will report it to the sender.

Chapter XII.

Whose spirit and supreme ruler Cabariel dwells toward that region of the world which is called Circius from the wind; he has under him seventy princes by day, and as many by night.

[unclear] twelfth dwelling of the described world, which is toward that region from which the wind Circius blows, Cabariel the great ruler inhabits with infinite spirits, among whom, for the operation of Steganography, fifty are appointed for the daytime and as many for the nighttime at all times; they preside over many and very powerful servants. Their secret office is to assist friends, disclose ambushes, and warn one who is absent of those against whom one must especially be on guard. From all these we shall name a few.

You now have, out of the hundred princes of the great Cabariel, twenty, and they are sufficient for you at present. The first ten of them are appointed for daytime operations with 500 servants, and the other ten for nighttime operations, likewise with their 500 attendants. And you should know that the spirits presiding over daytime operations are much more well disposed than the nighttime ones, and readier to obey, so that it is often necessary to compel the nighttime spirits themselves with a certain violence, and more often to repeat the conjuration. When commanded, they bring their servants with them; if they have not been ordered, they conceal them. When you wish to operate through the ministry of these spirits, turn yourself toward the region that we have mentioned and, after the customary preliminary things have been performed, say this conjuration:

Cabarielon ear chameron fruani, parnaton fofiel bryosi nagreal fabelrontyn adiel thortay nofruau pena afefiel chufy. When the song has been completed, if it is during the day, the spirit called will be present at once, without delay. But if it is at night and the spirit whom you have called delays in coming, press him as often as needed until he comes upon repetition of the song, which they are accustomed to revere greatly.

You send to your friend familiar letters or a devout prayer, which may bear being seen.

I had lent you my codex concerning the deeds of the Lombards, and Bede’s volume on the times, which you should return to me. For it befits a wise man, especially a Christian, everywhere to keep the faith he has promised. To forget benefits is held, by our divine and human institutions, to be a crime. Do not incur so sinful a guilt. I sent you my volumes so that you might restore them at some time. But I freely gave you the Greek books, in consideration of which you might deservedly show yourself more faithful to us by returning thanks. Farewell, from Spanheim, on the Ides of March, in the year of the Lord 1500.

When your friend has received these or any other letters sent by you, once he has recognized the sign of Cabariel, let him turn toward that quarter of the world from which the Circius wind proceeds; after first doing, according to custom, the things that must first be done, let him read this prayer in silence.

Of which the prince is called Raysiel, dwelling directly toward the North, under whom are fifty princes who preside over our daytime operations, and as many who [preside over] the nighttime ones; whose office is to announce transmissions.

[unclear] The thirteenth mansion is in the North, whose spirit and supreme emperor is Raysiel, who has under his dominion fifty dukes who preside over daytime operations, with many servants, and as many in number who preside over nighttime operations with their attendants. Their office is, in these matters and transmissions that pertain to death, to notify the friends of the operator and announce the secret. The dukes who preside over daytime operations obey the caller readily and come cheerful, joyful, and most ready to serve; but those who preside over nighttime operations are somewhat insolent, because they greatly hate and detest the light, nor do they easily obey, especially novices less proven in the art, whom they often mock to their face, unless they are so constrained by the operator’s conjurations that they cannot speak against him. For they greatly fear conjuration, and [unclear], they are given to being conjured more than the daytime spirits, and yet they obey unwillingly. But now from the number of all these let us set down the names of a few and the number of their servants, as many as suffice us for the customary operation.

You now have, excellent reader, out of the fifty diurnal princes, sixteen, with their servants, 670 in number; and out of the fifty nocturnal princes, fourteen, with their servants, 420 in number. These will suffice you for all operations, both nocturnal and diurnal. But when you wish to operate through them according to the intended hours, choose whichever one you wish from the arranged order, and summon him from the North, since they all dwell there, by this charm:

Charm of Conjuration.

R Aysiel astruano chameron fosiel onear Vemabi parnothon fruano Caspiel sufre bedarym bulifeor pean Curmaby Layr Vaymeor pesarym adoreꝰ odiel Vernabi peatha darsum lasphenō deuior Camedonton phorsy lasbenay to charmon druson olnays, Venouym lulefon, peorso fabelrōtos thurno. When the charm has been duly completed, and in silence, the summoned spirit will be present. Entrust the secret securely; he will carry out and report back what is to be entrusted. But if you see that those presiding over nocturnal operations, as they are generally accustomed to do, are delaying, compel them manfully by repeating the charm, fearing nothing; for they will be forced to reverence you as their lord.

I have a secret that I entrust to no one to carry, of this sort.

I posit the case. I have a certain friend, noble and learned, whom I know is to be killed secretly by certain assassins hired for pay. I do not dare warn him openly, because it is dangerous for me; in a more private family matter, I fear lest letters come into the hands of others; I do not presume to trust a man to speak it by mouth, because the one who is with me today may perhaps stand against me tomorrow. And so I take refuge in the customary art, by which, whatever I entrust to it, I do not fear will become public, even if it should happen to be tried by an enemy.

I send familiar letters to my friend, in which I fear no danger.

The ancients define Justice and Philosophy as the greatest ornament of nobility, and Impiety and Ignorance as its disgrace. For what is more beautiful than to adorn a noble family, which serves as a soldier, with letters and virtues? We find that very many others, and numerous very noble men serving as soldiers, did this by night and by day, so that they might subdue barbarians by arms, and by uprightness instruct their people and with letters. By their example, [Buma vv?], most learned, [unclear] the letters of humanity and the good arts [unclear], acknowledged, adorned with arms and letters. The wisest princes of old were accustomed not to shut up their wealth in their treasuries, but rather to devote it to literary use, judging the study of wisdom to be the most honorable support for those tending toward happiness, by which the blessedness of eternal retribution is acquired. Indeed, knowledge of the Scriptures makes princes venerable to all, and especially to be feared. Ignorance of the Scriptures, called the burial of a living man, has been accustomed to bring shame and horrible calamity upon noble princes. A man without letters is a two-footed ass, to be buried alive, or rather already buried. It is especially necessary that nobles who govern the commonwealth be wise and notable for knowledge of letters; their ignorance brings in tyranny. Love of letters also commends the renowned deeds of princes and nobles to perpetuity. For we see that ancient philosophers obtained the memory of rule, and attained immortality of name, everlasting among all men more by letters than by arms. For letters made the glorious, excellent, and wise ancient tyrants and princes more so than arms did, and endowed the memory and titles of their praises with immortality. Add that, for Christians, the study of letters provides the highest and most honorable aid for flying to Heaven. For from the Scriptures we begin to contemplate the flashing and honorable majesty of divine illuminations, to us
