Here we have five of Oriel’s dukes and ten of the counts, with the servants assigned to them in their turns, to the number of 1100, who suffice for us for every operation of this hour. But when you wish to work through them in this hour of the day, after first doing what must customarily be done beforehand, and after writing what must be written on clean paper, and arranging this conjuration on its back, do the rest as you know.

Conjuration.

Oriel burnadiel irasmy ersoty amear medusen. After you have completed this conjuration according to the proper instruction of the art, you will see the duke present with the other spirits called; entrust the secret to him.

Formulation of the Secret.

We have a friend whose welfare we favor; we fear that he is to be supplanted and circumvented by some wandering rogue. Therefore we desire that he be warned. We cannot do it in plain words by messengers; by letters, lest they fall into someone’s hands, likewise we dare not. Therefore, so that we may be safe and our secret may always remain hidden, let us call at least one spirit, the leader of those named above. He comes, obeys, and faithfully carries the message.

Let the letter be composed at pleasure.

Johannes Trithemius, Abbot of Sponheim, sends greetings to Heinrich von Bünau, golden knight, distinguished philosopher and mathematician.

Since you are a most devoted student of the humanities, you will rejoice, I think, exceedingly to have found a new companion in your studies. The man who will present this letter to you is a man of great knowledge, a supreme philosopher, a most subtle arithmetician, a most eloquent rhetorician, a very profound mathematician, and in every respect most excellently learned. He speaks with the greatest elegance, resplendent with Ciceronian eloquence. For if I were most especially your friend, I would have kept so great a man wholly to myself, since in using his services I have found him a most learned philosopher. I especially favor you; receive gladly the philosopher whom, moved by singular affection, I send to you. O would that all our students were such, who with timid heart scorn noble knowledge. This man constantly searches into the study of philosophy and the lofty sciences, and the most lofty and profound things of nature; he continually handles them and penetrates them most acutely. Therefore, Heinrich Bünau, remember for Christ’s sake to treat the man with a generous countenance. Farewell from Sponheim, 2 November, in the year of the Lord 1500.

When the friend to whom the letter is sent, skilled in this science of Steganography, has received the letter, let him do everything that according to the art must be done, and let him append the conjuration written above, as is customary. And when he has seen the spirit sent present, let him say these words to him, as the more powerful among the spirits: Camyn aparfy aslotiel omcar reneas vean triamy cralty penafon. When these have been uttered, the spirit will immediately draw nearer and will reveal the secret to him.

The appointment of any secret whatever.

We have a secret for a friend, or for anyone else skilled in our art, which we cannot signify either by letters or by a messenger, because we fear danger in either case. Therefore we call a spirit, entrust the secret to the stronger one, and in all things we are safe.

The tenor of the letters at pleasure.

Ioannes Trithemius, Abbot of Sponheim, of the Order of Saint Benedict, to Brother Quirinus, a monk of Corbie in France, greeting.

Concerning the mother of the perpetual Virgin Mary, I send my prayer, which you recently requested, Quirinus: Hail, most gracious mother Anna, most radiant parent of the Virgin Mary; you most faithful helper of all who call upon you; you noble refuge of those who seek you; quiet benefit of holiness. Hail, most gentle advocate of the poor; most beautiful consoler of those who groan; most adorned storehouse of virtues. Hail, [Iuda?], restorer of the sorrowful; most healthful medicine of the sick; and most celebrated promoter of faithful Christians. Obtain pardon for us as we pray; soften Christ, the dread judge; intercede for your servants, that we may attain blessedness; with you interceding, we ask that in his kindness he receive us miserable ones. Amen. The eighth day before the Ides of April, in the year of the Lord 1500.

When the person skilled in the art to whom the letters are sent has received them, let him first attend to the character of the hour attached to the letters; when this has been recognized, let him work through the lord of the ascendant of the hour in which he received the letters, together with the other things prescribed in the art. Then let him add the prayer written above, in the manner and order in which it is proper, and immediately the spirits sent will appear. When you have seen them, these words are to be spoken to the chief one among them: chamerusin maslotiel vear reneas liernoty trismy penafon. When these words have been spoken to the spirit stronger than the others, who is easily recognized from his habit and crown and always precedes the others, he will immediately reveal the secret into the ear.

The theme of any secret whatever, at pleasure, that occurs.

We have a friend absent far away. We know that a danger threatens him, of which he is unaware. We desire to warn him, but for certain reasons we do not dare to do so openly. Therefore we call the spirits assigned to this operation according to the hour, and safely commend the secret.

Letters, formed at pleasure, we seal with the sign of the spirit.

Everyone who glories in temporal things is by no means left to be called virtuous; and he who loves transitory things cannot be a lover of justice, since Catholic integrity detests a man gaping after desires. For the holy religion of the Christian faith forbids love of the world to its people, since he who loves worldly joys loses heavenly happiness. A Catholic who does not live as a Catholic is shown to have denied Christ; and he who loves temporal things is not called a good Catholic. He who loves the Creator seeks the joys of spiritual things. And when he has seen that the spirits, who will come without delay, are present, let him say to the more powerful one, who advances crowned: Famerusyn melyfno alny vemoby dreary drymes charfony. When these words have been spoken, the spirit will come nearer and will faithfully tell the secret into the ear of the operator. But he must be steadfast; they harm no one well instructed in the art. If, however, anyone of the unskilled should presume to approach, he would not escape danger.

Chapter XIII.

Whose hour is called Omalharien; its supreme angel is named Sabrathan, who has under his command many princes, dukes, counts, and servants.

The first hour of the night is called Omalharien; its angel is named Sabrathan, who has many other spirits under him, serving at various times in magical operations according to their orders, as Hermes and Solomon the Jew, most experienced in magic, attest. From these, many have been deputed in turn according to their orders for the operation of our art. For in the first order there are 10; in the second, 20; in the third, 30; in the fourth, 40; in the fifth, 500; in the sixth, 600; in the seventh, 70; in the eighth, 80; in the ninth, 90; in the tenth, 100. All these are sent into the service of secrets in their turns and hidden orders, about which we have neither full knowledge nor do we speak.

It is not safe to summon spirits in trivial causes; but where human services fail, let theirs be sought in the art.

A secret is made, whatever occurs to us, great and arduous.

The secret which we wish to communicate to a friend through spirits is made whatever may occur to us at the time and according to the variety of affairs, so that it is not trivial, nor of such a kind that it can otherwise be safely reported.

Johannes Trithemius, to the nuns on Mount Saint Rupert, who adorn the Catholic faith with bright virginity, continuously to merit eternal happiness by the most holy zeal of religion.

By the mercy of the eternal King, we providently send you, after he has been long awaited, a man of great experience in temporal affairs, Johannes, born of Raunenstat, for a long time reverend and zealous abbot of the monastery of Violsdorf, and freely resigning that same abbey. On his account, as I had promised you, I went to the monastery of Lunapurga, in which he was serving Christ, occupied with continual prayers and readings of the holy Scriptures, with the monks of that same monastery; and I asked that he come down to your convent and undertake the care of temporal affairs, and become procurator and cellarer. The abbot of Lympurg, with his usual instability, changed in mind, [unclear] I was able to obtain his consent to dismiss him. At last, by Christ’s inspiration, he consented, though fearfully, because he fears to serve nuns, who change very readily. He is not without reason afraid, since, as experience has taught us, nuns have sometimes repaid their stewards for benefits with a reward not praiseworthy. A feminine spirit suddenly [changes] into zeal of bitterness. Yet, with Christ granting it, I know that he will be useful to you. He is a Christian, he is a monk, he fears the Savior, and he is of good understanding. Therefore accustom yourselves to restrain feminine mutability, so that you may remember to be constant; receiving him with holy honor and sincere charity, laying aside every levity of feminine spirit, especially since, with the help of Christ the Redeemer, who is zealous for charity, he can assist you and restore the condition of temporal affairs collapsed in your monastery. Farewell. From Sponheim, 17 Kalends of May, in the year of our Lord Jesus Christ 1500.

to entrust to care: only when something occurs that you cannot safely make known to him either by letters or by messengers. For those things that we can make known without danger either by letters or by messengers, we must by no means make known through the ministry of spirits. But whoever shall try to summon spirits for light matters and secrets that can be made known without danger by letters or messengers will without doubt bring back loss and disadvantage, with danger.

The tenor of the letter, as one pleases.

To the venerable father in Christ, steward of the Lympurgenses, the religious lord called Johannes Weißdorffen, John Ouilis, humble abbot of Spanheim, joy of the heavens.

The nuns of Saint Rupert desire you with exceeding eagerness as their governor, and humbly ask you in goodwill to undertake the governance of the temporal affairs of that monastery. To serve the devout virgins of Christ is praiseworthy and meritorious. You have, in spiritual affairs of the same convent, an excellent and most renowned visitor, who embraces you with the greatest honor: grave in conduct, adorned with virtues, cautious in counsel, beloved by all, well reputed in the life of monastic religion, and notable to all men; and such a life is deservedly most pleasing to Christ: the excellent abbot of the monastery of Saint John. He is most learned, most studious, and most skilled in the writings both of Christians and of pagans, and he notably far surpasses the wisdom of all men. He knows very well how to govern the flock entrusted to him, and he is a very zealous guardian of the virgins of Christ, whose cloister he preserves most firmly. Do not fear to serve such honorable nuns under him, who knows how to govern the brides of Christ according to the monastic law with the best discretion. By the virtue and zeal of the Christian faith he will gladly come to your aid in necessity. Since you have this man, so famous and kindly, as an intimate friend, I profess that you should gladly assume the helm of so religious virgins. Christ will reward your labor with eternal joys. May the Bridegroom, protector, and most kindly rewarder of the nuns grant you, with good zeal, to strive after better things. Farewell. From Spanheim, 15 Kalends of May, in the year 1500.

When you have received letters marked with the Iesischa character, the person to whom they are sent, being skilled in the art, should first observe the lord of the ascendant of that hour with the whole figure of the sky, and should describe it on a clean sheet, and on its back the prescribed conjuration. When, after first doing what must be done beforehand, he has said it, and has seen the spirits sent to him standing present before him, let him say thus to the more powerful one in order: chamerusin aphroys aslotiel mean reneas vear tryamo cralti penason. When these words have duly been spoken to the principal spirit, he will approach nearer and will reveal in his ear the secret entrusted to him.

The Catholic faith saves no one who despises the ardor of divine love. To believe and not to have zeal for divine love is of no use at all for the redemption of the soul. Moreover, many people are now found who boast of the Catholic faith, but few have the works of the Christian faith; but idle faith dies. Many believe, but very few observe the commandments of God. Alas, the zeal of believers is weak; even unbelieving people can have a stronger zeal than this, and many do have it. Gentiles and people who do not believe that our savior, made man, is the son of the Almighty will be tormented by the punishments of hell. But all those who believe that the Son of God came into the world and became man through zeal for human redemption, yet do not adorn the Christian faith with holy works, and, always entangled in sins, prefer the honors of the world to eternal blessedness, zealously pursuing impious actions and staining the purity of faith with corrupt morals against obedience, will be tortured with heavier punishments. But the lovers of God, who have the right zeal of the Christian faith, prefer nothing to God, imitate Christ, flee sins, and despise the riches and honors of the world. Now therefore attend to these words, you who glory in faith: love God, and you will have the reward of blessedness, pursuing righteousness. If you love the vanities of the age against the honor of God, you will receive the prize of those who pursue iniquity: the horrors of hell. Written on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of May, in the year of the Lord 1500.

Book Two.

The secret may be of whatever kind.

Concerning the announcing of a secret to a friend, absent near or far, who is already skilled in this art of spirits, it matters little what sort it is, provided it is not slight, or such as could otherwise have been safely announced by messengers or letters. We are also not concerned what the letters are like, provided they have the character of the principal angel of that hour in which the operation is performed: no secret at all.

Let us form letters at pleasure.

Johannes Trithemius, Abbot, sends greeting to Nicolaus Basselius, monk, and transmits this prayer of Saint Nicholas.

Creator of all things, reformer and maker, created the first man, Adam, to whom he joined a very beautiful wife named Eve, the mother of all living things, prefiguring the Catholic Church, to be joined to shepherds, shining beautifully with the morals of uprightness, and destined to bear sons of good works, men who by humility obtain the kingdoms of heaven that will remain without end. Christ redeemed us through his most kindly love for us; he gave us the Catholic faith, and those who truly love it will rightly obtain angelic happiness. Therefore let us all, living in true religion and living as Catholics, daily honor our almighty creator. Lord Jesus, most kindly savior, who mercifully redeemed us all from the abyss of death, kindly regarding our frailty and weakness, conform us to the Catholic faith, so that after this transitory life we may deserve to have forever the rest of eternal consolation and happiness. Amen. 14 Kalends of May, in the year of the Lord 1500.

When you have received these letters, marked with the character of Mendrion, the person to whom they are sent, being skilled in our art, should observe the lord of the ascendant; let him write both it and the whole disposition of the sky on a clean sheet, and on its back the conjuration. Then, after adding all the things that must be added, and after the chant has been spoken, as soon as the spirit has seen his altar, let him say these words to the first one: Chamerusyn merion nodiel burmy raueto elay reas penafon.

When he has sounded these words to him who appears to be the more eminent among the other spirits, immediately he will approach calmly and will reveal the secret entrusted to him.

Chapter 20.

Whose hour is called Xymalim, and its angel, the supreme emperor, is called Narcoriel, having under him princes, dukes, counts, and servants.

The eighth hour of the night is called Xymalim. Its angel, the first supreme emperor, is called Narcoriel, who has under his command many other spirits, princes, dukes, ministerial counts, who in their orders are called to various effects by those who work in the secrets of philosophy. And from all these there are twelve orders of those who serve Steganography. In the first order there are 10; in the second 20; in the third 30; in the fourth 40; in the fifth 50; in the sixth 60; in the seventh 70; in the eighth 80; in the ninth 90; in the tenth 100; in the eleventh 10,000. All these observe their orders in such a way that no one can safely work through them unless he has been fully instructed in all things. For whoever does not observe the due order exposes himself to danger and will be frustrated of the desired effect.

Therefore when you wish to operate through them in Steganography at the eighth hour of the night, observe the lord of the ascendant, and write both it and the whole disposition of the sky on clean paper, and on its back, with the other things customarily used according to custom, this conjuration.

Conjuration.

Narconiel aples pornya nauelo meas. Triome ilneas azyfan lafias my bression ersoti penason. Then, after the things to be added according to custom have been added, and after the conjuration has been spoken, the spirits summoned will be present in that form which you have instructed them to assume, ready for all things.

Secret argument.

The secret that we wish to learn from a friend far absent, if we trust neither letters nor couriers: let us entrust it in the eighth hour of the night to one of the more powerful spirits of Narcoriel, fearing absolutely nothing, since all are faithful and most ready for obedience.

Of Steganography

Let us form letters at will.

O most gracious Jesus, I give thanks to your most holy mercy: you who by your blood reconciled the human race to the heavenly Father, hanging piteously raised upon the Cross; you subjected for our sake the flourishing youth of your most noble body to harsh wounds, so that you might make dead man live. Therefore, let us Catholics give such thanks as we can to our redeemer: groaning and praising, recalling in Christian fashion the memory of the passion of the savior of our race. Have mercy on me, most merciful Jesus, fount of mercy, abyss of compassion, glory of the saints, light of the citizens above; and pour into me the sweetest taste of your most holy love. Deliver me from all my calamities. Give me true gladness of heart, that I may exult in your praises, glorifying you, since by the pain of your wounds you have healed me. What shall I render to your mercy, my Redeemer, my giver of life? I have compassion for your sufferings with burning tears, and, blessing the most holy wounds of your body, most gracious Savior Jesus, I give thanks, asking pardon for my crimes. In the year of the Lord 1500, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of May, I wrote this prayer, τυμβοὶ λαοῦ τε γῆ μου.

When the person to whom letters, of whatever sort they may be, marked with the character of Narcoriel, have been sent receives them, being skilled in the art, let him observe the lord of the ascendant at that same hour, and write both it and the whole disposition of the heavens, with the rest, on a clean sheet; and when all necessary things have been added beneath according to custom, and the said conjuration has been spoken, when he sees that the spirits stand by him, let him say these words to the more powerful one: Medaro Castotiel va reneas thafny thyrmo thea penason. When these have been said according to the instruction of this art, immediately the chief spirit will come nearer and will disclose the secret word.

Then, when everything prescribed in the art has been completed, say the conjuration itself, taking the greatest care not to omit anything required for the perfection of the operation. When the conjuration has been spoken, the named spirits will at once appear visibly in the form which you ordered them to assume. For all whom we have named are benevolent, good, prompt, and willingly obedient to one who operates duly, and faithful in the tasks entrusted to them.

Subject of the Secrets.

Whatever secret occurs to us, which otherwise we cannot safely make known to a friend either by letters or by messengers, we first entrust to the spirits appearing to us, and we are secure. The more eminent one among the others is distinguished by the appearance of a crown.

Let the letters be formed at will.

Wail, mortals, you who now laugh: by your very grave sins and horrible crimes you have in many ways most ungratefully spurned the kindness also of our glorious redeemer. Behold, the Turk, the deadly enemy of Christians, will move his army from Hungary; he will slaughter men like beasts. Savage, kindled with zeal for impiety as if with fire, he has crossed the Danube. Therefore mourn, most wretched ones, doomed to die in horrible slaughter; you will die in bitter zeal, because your crimes will seize you. You have despised the laws of God, your most gracious redeemer. Therefore you will be handed over to most cruel enemies, who will devour you like locusts. We have heard how cruelly the Turk invaded Hungary, Bohemia, and Poland; he destroyed very strong cities; women and virgins consecrated to God, holding chastity in zeal for holiness, he most shamefully violated, horribly slaughtering all Catholic men, raging everywhere like cruel beasts. The intention of any secret whatsoever.

Let the secret be whatever it may. When you cannot make it known by letters and messengers to a friend living near or far, summon one or two from the spirits Iasguarim and appoint them as your couriers; entrust the secret, doubting nothing.

Book Two.

Letters are to be formed at will.

This is the prophecy of Nicolaus Basselius of Hirsau, bishop and saint, which he saw in Spicatus. And he said: Thus says the Lord to the shepherds of the churches. Soon you will perish, because a very great calamity will scatter your broad dominion and will sprinkle all Europe. Woe to the Ishmaelites, who break the covenants of the tabernacle, because through envy and rashness they seize Easter. Behold, the dominion that you have will be broken unless you hasten greater repentance; and you will be handed over to be torn apart. Alas, the whole Church has been overturned by the worst morals; pretense has invaded its ministers. Flee; do not look back. You will be laid waste, and you will be dragged by dogs; they will sprinkle the whole land with blood. Therefore, inhabitants of the earth, do penance. Young Benjamin will experience disturbances. Woe to the inhabitants of Gennesaret, which is Europe, because on account of the multitude of their sins they will perish under the hands of the Bulgarians. Here ends the prophecy of Nicolaus, bishop of Hirsau, 12 Kalends of May.

When letters of whatever kind, marked beforehand with the sign Iasguarim, have been received by the person to whom they are sent, one skilled in the art should do everything that is prescribed according to the art, and should observe the order of the planets, and write what must be written. And when the conjuration written above has been spoken, immediately, when the spirits have appeared mingled together, let him say to the first among them: Chamerusin othriel arnotiel solais elty. Naeles proy vear sato cralnoti, penason. When these words have been said, the spirit, immediately approaching, will faithfully and calmly reveal the message entrusted to him.

The secret to be entrusted.

All the above-mentioned dukes and counts are good and faithful, doing harm to absolutely no one who loves God in truth. Therefore entrust to them whatever you wish to announce, according to the art, at the second hour of the night to a friend absent near or far, doubting nothing.

V Ioan.

154 Of the Steganography of Johannes Trithemius, Abbot of Sponheim. To Cornelius Gyrardus of Gouda, canon of St. Augustine near Leiden, greetings.

Our Lord Jesus Christ, the most gentle savior of our souls, promised us the happiness of eternal consolation, if [unclear] his commandments with a pure [unclear]. Dearest brother, keep diligently the commandments of God and of the holy rule, because unless you preserve inviolate until death all the things that almighty God has commanded you, you will perish by eternal death. Therefore I have handed on to you the form and law of a religious and holy way of life.

Beware, then, diligently, lest you give your heart to be possessed by any mortal creature through the desire of love, because no one comes to those highest joys except the one who despises the world for God. Again, therefore, through this letter of mine I exhort you, as my dearest friend, to observe the warnings that I had given you. For I think that I am doing something good when I write something good in this sacred time, especially for edification concerning the manner of living well, by which you may always become better. Therefore now again I write to you for your good, because I fear your danger no less than my own. But I beg you: always keep watch, advancing daily in the fear of God, and living innocent, harming no one, and altogether persevering in your holy purpose. Do not trust in time, nor fortune, nor age, because they are nothing but smoke. Truly I love you sincerely in Christ Jesus, praying that he himself may arrange that I also be beloved to you; and that I, who am absent from you in body, may always be present in spirit. Therefore, since I continually keep remembrance of you in my prayers, I very earnestly beg you not to forget me. Farewell. 12 Kalends of May, in the year 1500.

Chapter.

Book Two.

Chapter XXIV.

Whose hour is called Xephan, and its angel, called the supreme emperor, is Sarandiel, having under him many princes, dukes, counts, and servants.

The twelfth hour of the night, which reaches the dawn, is called Xephan, and its angel is called Sarandiel, who has under his command many spirits, good and evil, princes, dukes, counts, and ministers, who are assigned to various operations: the good to good ones, and the evil to evil ones. These princes, as Hermes the Hebrew, who is called Solomon, says in the fourth book on the offices of spirits, are accustomed often to appear in that form in which the Devil is read to have appeared to Eve, having one beautiful head like that of a maiden, with hair hanging down on either side, but two serpent-bodies, which nevertheless they always veil and hide under certain coverings or leaves, so that they may not be seen. In face, however, they are most beautiful, benevolent, and pleasant, and most ready and cheerful for every obedience to the operator.

IN QVO DOCEBIMVS MODVM ET FOR- mam generalem accedendi ad hanc artem Steganographiae, et operandi in ea sine periculo, cum maxima vtilitate. QVICVNQVE adhuius artis nostrae occultae scienti- am accedere desiderat: quicunque operari per eam mirabilia et multis commodo sa periculis optat: in- primis oportet eum ornatum esse virtutibus, et con- scientiae mundae, ac voluntatis bonae, ad Deum, ad seipsum et ad proximum: ne sit inclinatus ad nocendum alicui, neque com- mercia turpitudinis querat. Consequenter ne cesse est, vt praeceptorem habeat in arte perfectum et expertum: quia non nisi paucis et in multis eruditiissimis, et maxime in ma- gicis peritis ad hanc scientiam venire sine praeceptore possibile credimus. Arrangement for Sending a Secret Message.

When you see the spirits standing before you in a strange form, do not be afraid, because they are good and benevolent, harming no one, and they almost always conceal a monstrous form, lest they terrify anyone, appearing with a very beautiful face. Safely entrust whatever, in the hour of the night, you wish [to write to a friend?]. Let the letters be formed as you please.

O wretched man, and truly pitiable, why do you not attend to the instability of all temporal things? And why do you not consider that you will shortly die? Remember what the first man deserved because he violated the commandment. Would that, as Balaam wished, our soul might die the death of the righteous, so that, scorning present pleasures and the vain honors of the world, we may be unstained, keeping ourselves from every sin. But we do not take care, until at last we fall into the dreadful bonds of death, to be tormented forever. I consider happy the man who thinks of these things beforehand. Therefore, O man, cast away the world, as the Son of God did, and consider how many evils follow us from love of it. For many dangers are brought upon us, and because it is damnable to those who love it, it is rightly despised. Worthy of eternal death is the lover of the world. What does that world profit you, wretched man? When it is loved, it flees; while it is present, it passes away; while it exalts, it [unclear]; while it flatters, it deceives; while it flourishes, it withers; when it sends forth its lovers, it hands them over to perpetual miseries. Chapter 25.

In which we shall teach the general method and form of approaching this art of Steganography, and of operating in it without danger, with the greatest usefulness.

Whoever desires to approach the knowledge of this hidden art of ours; whoever wishes to work wonders through it, and things useful to many amid dangers: first of all he must be adorned with virtues, and be of clean conscience and good will toward God, toward himself, and toward his neighbor, so that he is not inclined to harm anyone, nor seeks dealings of baseness. Then it is necessary that he be somewhat imbued with the good arts of letters, and especially with the science of the stars, so that he may know the general motions, courses, wanderings, changes, orders, natures, positions, risings, settings, and effects of the stars, signs, and planets; because without competent knowledge of these no one can have access to the depths of this art. Consequently it is necessary that he have a teacher perfect and experienced in the art, because we believe it possible to come to this science without a teacher only for a few, and for those most learned in many things, and especially skilled in magical matters. But the teacher must be not only proven and experienced in knowledge, but also faithful, upright, and fearing God; because the purer he has been in good conduct with God, the safer he will be in the operation of this science. For the spirits obey virtues. Therefore, when anyone is about to approach this art, let the teacher receive him and lead him into some secret and clean place. Let the time be tranquil and clear, and

Of the Steganography ... and the moon in complete opposition, with the sun shining clearly; and let Mercury be in the ascendant, joined to Venus or Jupiter, if possible; and let Saturn and Mars be remote, because if they themselves, or either of them, are with the ascendant, the initiation will not be perfect. First of all the person to be initiated in the art shall swear an oath: I, N., swear and promise by the power of almighty God, by the blood of our Lord Jesus Christ, by the resurrection of the dead and the last judgment, and by the salvation of my soul in the holy Catholic faith, to almighty God, to the blessed Virgin Mary, to all the saints, and to you, N., that I will faithfully keep this art of Steganography hidden all the days of my life, nor will I teach it to anyone without your will and consent. Moreover, by the same power I swear and promise that I will not use this science against God and his commandments, nor against the holy Roman and universal Church or its ministers, nor against justice and equity. So may God help me, and so may he save me at the last judgment. Then the preceptor shall read the following conjuration in the mystical tongue, and shall interpret it, and all the conjurations contained in this work, before the disciple, lest he suspect that there is anything diabolical, superstitious, or contrary to God, or that any compact with demons, implicit or explicit, is in any way secretly hidden there.

And after the master of this art has explained to his disciple the conjuration, order, and series of all the spirits, he shall reveal to him the most secret mysteries of this science, which are neither written nor to be written, forbidding him under the oath he has taken to reveal them to anyone as long as he lives, except to worthy persons sworn in the art, or to write them in any manner or for any reason. Then he shall teach him the natures, names, places, numbers, offices, and properties of all the spirits who are assigned to this art: how, when, and where work is to be done through them, and the remaining mysteries that pertain to the perfection of this art, concerning which nothing is to be written.

Here ends the second book of the Steganography of Johannes Trithemius, Abbot of Sponheim, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of May, in the year of the Lord 1500.

Here begins the third book of the Steganography of Johannes Trithemius, Abbot of Sponheim, addressed to the most serene prince, Lord Philip, Count Palatine of the Rhine, Duke of Bavaria, and Prince Elector of the Holy Empire.

Preface.

After, with the aid of our Lord Jesus Christ, Savior of faithful souls, we had completed the first two books of our art, in which we described our Steganography as best we could, we must join this third book to them, and link more marvelous things to marvelous discoveries. I found in a certain book of a certain ancient philosopher, who was called Menaistor, that it is possible, by a certain art, for us to make known the conception of our mind to a friend, however absent he may be, without hours, without words, without books, and without a messenger, most perfectly, most broadly, and most secretly. And since I was driven very vehemently by a desire to know, I began to wish to test the truth of the statements; and after many labors at last I found that very science proven by experience. Very great is

Ego autem metuens, tam mirabile opus propter nimiam obscuritatem vilipendi ab impe- ritis, aut tandem igni cremari: cum in eo multis probationibus iam diu sim expertus: ita illud literis commendare apertioribus volui, vt et amp; viris eruditis ac in magicis studiosissimis, cum Dei auxilio, possit aliquatenus fieri peruium: &amp; tamen imperitis Rapophagis omni tempore maneat occultatum, &amp; nullatenus eorum obtuso intellectui cognitum. Isti sunt septem Angelorum traditionem an- tiquorum sapientum, quorum quilibet ducit Mundum annis trecen- tis quinquaginta quatuer mensibus bis binis in ordine suo. Orifiel est Angelus Saturni, qui à principio creationis gubernauit Mundum annis 354 mensibus 4. Postea Venus, deinde Iuppiter, post illum Mercurius, ac deinde Mars, posteia Luna, postem Sol. Quilibet annis 354. mensibus 4. suum Angelum in tabula sibi communi scri- ptum dominium Mundi habuisse describitur. Itaque tempore diluuij ferunt sapientes Samaelem Angelum Martis seruiuisse Imperio re- giminis: Gabrielem autem Angelum Lunae tempore confusionis lin- guarum: Michaelem Angelum Solis, tempore exitus Jsraelis de AE- gypto Et quidem si quis assertioni praefatae adhibet fidem, per semet ab origine Mundi facile mutationes temporum, &amp; gubernationem Angelorum vsque ad suam aetatem praescripto ordine poterit suppu- tare. Nos autem ea, quae nostro conducunt proposito, profequentes, Septem Angelis planetarum predictis 21. subiectos alios spiritus, hoc est, vnicuique tres non ambigimus secundum huiufmodi artis no- strae institutionem: per quos intentionis nostrae operamur effectum. Ordinem planetarum consuetum obseruabimus, à supremo omnium Saturno incipientes vsque ad Lunam: primo cuiuslibet principalis angeli operationem conscribentes, ac deinde subseruientium: &amp;amp; capitula per ordinem con- iungentes. Preface.

The secret of this art is of such a kind, and wrapped in such great obscurities, that it is not easily accessible to anyone. For Menastor enveloped the mystery very obscurely and in few words, and he used such powers to keep it secret that after him no one has yet been found who has dared to make his discourse clearer by any instruction. But I, fearing that so marvelous a work, because of its excessive obscurity, might be despised by the unskilled, or at last burned in the fire, since I have long since tested it by many proofs, wished to commit it to writing in clearer letters, so that, with God's help, it might in some measure become accessible to learned men and to those most devoted to magical studies; and yet it should at all times remain hidden from unskilled Rapophagi, and in no way become known to their dull understanding.

But Menastor said: There are seven planets, over which seven angels preside, and under them are subject twenty-one spirits, through whom secrets are announced. Let us set out their names by means of a table.

Preface.

These are the seven angels, according to the tradition of the ancient sages, each of whom guides the world for three hundred fifty-four years and four months in his order. Orifiel is the angel of Saturn, who from the beginning of creation governed the world for 354 years and 4 months. Afterwards Venus, then Jupiter, after him Mercury, and then Mars, afterwards the Moon, afterwards the Sun. Each is described as having held dominion over the world for 354 years and 4 months, with his angel written in the table common to him. And so the sages report that at the time of the flood Samael, the angel of Mars, served the authority of rule; Gabriel, however, the angel of the Moon, at the time of the confusion of tongues; Michael, the angel of the Sun, at the time of Israel's departure from Egypt. And indeed, if anyone gives credence to the aforesaid assertion, he will easily be able by himself, from the origin of the world down to his own age, to calculate the changes of times and the governance of the angels in the order prescribed. But we, pursuing those things that serve our purpose, do not doubt that under the seven aforesaid angels of the planets there are subject twenty-one other spirits, that is, three to each one, according to the instruction of this art of ours; through them we accomplish the effect of our intention. We shall observe the customary order of the planets, beginning from Saturn, the highest of all, down to the Moon, first writing down the operation of each principal angel, and then of those serving under them, and joining the chapters together in order.

SATVRNVS, planetarum omnium altior supre- mus motu natura tardus, frigidus, quia remotus, difficilis, grauis, à puncto sui principii 650. annis vf- que ad punctum primae stationis in quolibet signe mensibus cõmorans 30.naturali proprio mouetur 626. E- ius primus supremus Angelus vocatur, secũdum opinionem antiquorum, Orifiel, qui habet sub se alios tres principales Spiri- tus, videlicet Sadael, Poniel Morisiel, de quibus suo dicemus loco ordine. Per hunc autem Orifielem magnum Saturni Angelum fiunt multae diuersae operationes in Steganogra- phia.Per ipsum possumus mentis nostrae arcanum notum face- re amico,artem scienti, vbicunque fuerit:per literas, si placet: vel etiam sine literis alia multa mirabilia facere,quae nemo in- telligit alius, qui in hac nostra scientia imperitus fuerit. Itaque volens per hunc Angelum in Steganographia quippiam opera- ri,maxime in die Saturni, in his rebus,negociis causis, quae pertinent ad Saturnum:in primis necesse est, vt motus eius no- ueris varios diuerfos. Et varios primum, purum, proprium, mixtum,rectum,retrogradum confusum. Et in his omnibus non solum generales regulas ab Astronomis traditas (quia licet maxime conducant huic scientiae nostrae, tamen non penitus sufficiunt) sed etiam particulares sciat necesse est. Pro funda- mente igitur praesuppositis tabulis regulis de motibus plane- tarum, quos omnino scire operãtem in haec arte necessarium est: specia- LIBERTIVS. 165 speciales regulas et tabellas punctualium motuum per singula capitula huius operis adiecimus, sine quarum obseruatione ne- mo in hac arte poterit operari. Et nota, quod dies cuiuslibet pla- netae in quatuor partes aequales diuiditur, quarum primam, i ko- ras inaequales tres angelus ipsius planetae principalis obtinet: &amp; reliquas tres partes eius substituti per ordinem consequuntur. Tertias te- net Pomiel secundus : &amp; quartas tres horas Morisiel Angelus Orifielis tertius. Sub primis tribus horis dici tam Saturni quam caeterarum stellarum in rebus Saturno appropriatis operandum est per Orifielem: sub secundis per Sadaelem: sub tertijs per Po- mielem: &amp; sub vltimis tribus per Morifielem. Chapter I

On Orifiel, the first and supreme angel of Saturn, and on the operations that are performed through him.

Saturn, the highest and supreme of all the planets, slow in motion and by nature, cold because remote, difficult, heavy, from the point of its beginning 650 years up to the point of its first station, remaining in each sign for 30 months, is moved by its natural proper motion 626. Its first and supreme angel is called, according to the opinion of the ancients, Orifiel, who has under him three other principal spirits, namely Sadael, Poniel, and Morisiel, of whom we shall speak in their proper place and order.

Through this Orifiel, the great angel of Saturn, many different operations are performed in steganography. Through him we can make the secret of our mind known to a friend who knows the art, wherever he may be: by letters, if one wishes, or even without letters, and do many other marvelous things, which no one else understands who is unskilled in this science of ours. Therefore, anyone wishing to perform anything through this angel in steganography, especially on the day of Saturn, in these matters, business, and causes that pertain to Saturn, must first know its various and diverse motions. And first the various motion: pure, proper, mixed, direct, retrograde, and confused. And in all these he must know not only the general rules handed down by the astronomers, because although they are very useful for this science of ours, nevertheless they do not wholly suffice, but also the particular rules.

Therefore, once the tables and rules concerning the motions of the planets have been laid down as a foundation, which anyone working in this art must know completely, we have added special rules and tables of punctual motions throughout the individual chapters of this work; without observing them no one will be able to operate in this art. And note that the day of each planet is divided into four equal parts, of which the principal angel of that planet obtains the first, that is, three unequal hours; and his substitutes in order take the remaining three parts. For example: on the day of Saturn, Orifiel, its first angel, possesses the three unequal hours from sunrise, which are called the hours of the planets; Sadael, his first angel, possesses the second three; Pomiel, the second, holds the third; and Morisiel, the third angel of Orifiel, holds the last three hours. In the first three hours of the day both of Saturn and of the other stars, in matters appropriated to Saturn, one must operate through Orifiel; in the second, through Sadael; in the third, through Pomiel; and in the last three, through Morisiel. And all operations, according to the motion of Saturn, receive either a prosperous effect or a weak one. But now let us set down the punctual table.

Medio motu Saturni in secundum diem, gradum et horam ex tabulis communibus cognito, diligenter inprimis obseruãdum scias, vtrum fit directus an retrogradus; purus, proprius, mixtus aut confusus. Hoc autẽ ex tabulis communibus non inuenies. Id circo praescriptam tabulam ordinauimus, in qua punctum principij motus eius finis poteris inuenire qualibet hora, diuisis gradibus fit nul intercurrentibus in particulis minutorũ. Ita videlicet ad quodlibet minutũ in duas, tres vel quatuor partes horarias secundum proportionem motus puri aut confusi, hoc est, aliorum planeta rum coniunctione separatione obseruata, diuidatur: im possibile est enim vel per stellas vel per Spiritus stellatum te pofle ad effectum huius artis perueneri, nisi motu punctuali cognitio diligentissime obseruato tuas operationes ad qualitates planetarum proprias noueris pręcise ordinare. Nam in diuerfis gradu bus, signis, diebus, horis, minutis, secundis, ter tijs quartis planeta rum effectus, quo ad hanc scientiam, diuer fimode variantur. In quolibet enim gradu 25. mutationes diuersas obseruauirmus inuenimus: vnde quemlibet gradum in totidem partes diuidere principales necessarium nobis videbatur. Ista autem diuisio non habet locum per omnes gradus, sed in illis duntaxat, in quibus stellę nobis ad hanc artem cõducentes oriuntur, cum qui bus fit operatio ad significandum absentibus omne, quod volum us, ministerio Spirituum fine literis, sicut dicemus. Itaque prima tabula diuisionis graduum motus Saturni, quam praemissimus, primae quartae diei vel noctis deseruit perpetuo in his, quae pertinet ad operationem Saturni principũ eius; secunda vero ad sectandas tres horas, tertia ad tertias, quarta ad quartas. Deinde subiecumus punctualem ordinẽ motus ipfius Saturni in ascendente, quando videlicet fuerit in vnox ex primis quatuor signis, cujus sunt Aries, Taurus, Gemini Cancer. Of Steganography.

When the mean motion of Saturn for the second day, degree, and hour has been learned from the common tables, know that it must first be carefully observed whether it is direct or retrograde; pure, proper, mixed, or confused. But you will not find this from the common tables. For that reason we have arranged the prescribed table, in which you will be able to find the point of the beginning and [end?] of its motion at any hour, the degrees being divided, with intervening [unclear], into particles of minutes. That is, each minute is to be divided into two, three, or four hourly parts, according to the proportion of the pure or confused motion, that is, with the conjunction or separation of the other planets observed. For it is impossible, either through the stars or through the spirits of the stars, for you to arrive at the effect of this art unless, with the knowledge of the punctual motion most diligently observed, you know how to order your operations precisely according to the proper qualities of the planets. For in different degrees, signs, days, hours, minutes, seconds, thirds, and fourths, the effects of the planets, with respect to this science, vary in different ways. For in each degree we have observed and found twenty-five different changes; hence it seemed necessary to us to divide each degree into just as many principal parts. This division, however, does not apply throughout all the degrees, but only in those in which the stars conducive to this art rise for us, with which the operation is performed for signifying to the absent everything that we wish, by the ministry of spirits, without letters, as we shall say. Therefore the first table of the division of the degrees of the motion of Saturn, which we have set forth above, serves perpetually for the first quarter of the day or night in those things which pertain to the operation of Saturn and its beginnings; the second, however, for the second three hours; the third for the third; the fourth for the fourth. Then we have added the punctual order of the motion of Saturn itself in the ascendant, namely when it shall have been in one of the first four signs, which are Aries, Taurus, Gemini, and Cancer. We shall also arrange a following table concerning the remaining eight signs.

Deinde in eadem secũda tabula motum Saturni in quolibet duodecim signorum ad omnes quartas diei et amp; noctis ita digessimus ad minutias, vt qualibet hora nobis gradu ascendentis, in quo fuerit Saturnus ipse, cognito, clare pate- scere possit radix ipsius punctualis, semel autem terminata calculatur alicuius quod nostra aetas nescio si vnquam pertingere possit, tabula denuo à capite sui principij incipienda est. In tertia tabula septenariam coniunctionem Saturni cum caeteris planetis, quae vnica est, ad proportionẽ reduximus: per quam o- mnes coniunctiones 120. facile ad punctum reducuntur. In ea- dem tabula purus motus planetarum omnium per punctualem principij cuiuslibet diuisionem, progressionem et amp; elongationẽ à puncto in quolibet motu cognoscitur, si medius motus antea perfecte habeatur. Nã sine cognitione medij motus impossibi- le est aliquem ad practicam huius scientiae posse accedere. Rur- sus etiamsi medium motum et amp; verum similiter perfectissime intellegas, nihil tibi ad huius scientiae cognitionem proderit, nisi praescriptas tres tabulas ad omnes punctos divisionũ in motibus planetatum à gradibus inaequalibus aequaliter sumptos per mi- nutias singulas ad integrum intelligas. Sed iam ad operationem procedamus. Cognitis autem omnibus, intellectisque perfecte his, quae di- ximus, &amp; auxiliante Deo, dicturi sumus: cum volueris in hac pro- fundissima speculatione operari : in primis oportet te scire or- tum exaltationem et amp; occasum omnium stellarum octauae Sphae- rae, per quas fit operatio: &amp; quantum quaelibet distet ab alia. Sunt autem Stellae, per quas operamur ad nunciãdum secretũ quod- cunque absenti siue verbis siue scriptis et amp; sine homine nuncio, septengentae numero, quarum nomina, loca, ortus, occasus, ele- uationes, distantias, accessus et amp; regressus in libro speciali descri- psimus, quos nimis studiosum esset hic denuo inferendo repe- tere. Itaque obseruata stellae in omnibus sicut oportet, &amp; cogni- to puncto ascendentis in quo Saturnus eadem hora fuerit, si per ipsum fit operatio: diligentissime considera qualitatem motui- Y 3 psius [illegible]

at the degree of Aries, point 641, [unclear] and 69, we have included the whole Zodiac in the second table. Then, in the same second table, we have arranged the motion of Saturn in any one of the twelve signs, for all the quarters of the day and night, down to the minutes, so that, at whatever hour, once the degree of the ascendant in which Saturn himself is has been known by us, the precise root of it may be able to appear clearly. But once the calculation of something has been completed, to which I do not know whether our age can ever attain, the table must be begun anew from the head of its beginning. In the third table we have reduced to proportion the sevenfold conjunction of Saturn with the other planets, which is unique; through it all 120 conjunctions are easily reduced to the point. In the same table the pure motion of all the planets is known through the punctual division of each beginning, progression, and elongation from the point in any motion, if the mean motion has first been perfectly obtained. For without knowledge of the mean motion it is impossible for anyone to be able to approach the practice of this science. Again, even if you understand the mean motion and likewise the true motion most perfectly, it will profit you nothing for knowledge of this science unless you understand fully the three prescribed tables for all the points of the divisions in the motions of the planets, taken equally from unequal degrees, minute by minute. But now let us proceed to the operation.

When, however, all these things have been known, and those things which we have said, and, with God’s help, are going to say, have been perfectly understood, when you wish to work in this most profound speculation, first of all you must know the rising, elevation, and setting of all the stars of the eighth sphere, through which the operation is made, and how far each is distant from another. The stars through which we operate for announcing any secret whatever to an absent person, whether by words or by writings and without a human messenger, are seven hundred in number. Their names, places, risings, settings, elevations, distances, approaches, and recessions we have described in a special book; it would be too laborious to repeat them here again by inserting them. Therefore, when the star has been observed in all respects as is proper, and when the point of the ascendant in which Saturn was at that same hour has been known, if the operation is made through him, consider most diligently the quality of its motion

LIBERTIVS. 175 rentiori ante te super mensam aut pulpitum. Et de coniuratio- nem ad Spiritum, per quem operaris, sibi appropriatam. Aut si malueris sine scriptis omnino nunciare secretum per Spiritum, vel sine Spiritu, in tuo arbitrio sic positum. Eiusdem namque o- perationis est, cum Spiritu vel sine Spiritu secretum nunciare a- mico, paucis alteratis, sicut suo loco dicemus. Iam differentia o- perationum Saturni et Angelorum eius secundū quatuor quar- tas principales cum coniurationibus vnicuique per ordinem appropriatis componemus: quibus vtendum est, cum per Spiri- tum nuncios arcanum. De primo Angelo Saturni, qui est principalis, & vocatur O- rifiel, qui primam quartam Saturni obseruat. PRIMVS et amp; principalis angelus Saturni, sicut in prae- cedentibus diximus, vocatur Orifiel, qui cum caere- ris angelis planetarum in ordine suo orbem regit annis 354 mensibus quatuor. Hic habet primam partem tam in die, quam in nocte: &amp; per eum fit operatio ab or- tu Solis in die, &amp; ab occasu Solis in nocte, vsque ad tertiam horā inclusiue in omnibus, quae ad Saturnum pertinent, &amp; in eius die ac nocte, sicut diximus. Cum itaqꝫ in prima quarta Saturni ali- quid volueris nuntiare absenti sine verbis et amp; sine literis: tum Spiritus Saturni non alius, quam Orifiel, tibi vocandus est: quia per eum poteris omnia nunciare perfectissime. Inpri- mis considera, in quo signo sit iste Saturnus, &amp; in quo gradu, &amp; an sit directus vel retrogradus, &amp; quibus planetis sit con- iunctio. De primo ponamus exemplum: Ecce Saturnus iam est in 25. grad. Tauri, die 28. mensis Aprilis anni praesentis, qui est Domini 1500. LIBERTIUS.

[unclear] before you on the table or lectern. And concerning the conjuration appropriated to the Spirit through whom you work. Or, if you prefer to announce the secret entirely without writings, through the Spirit or without the Spirit, this is placed at your discretion. For it is an operation of the same kind to announce a secret to a friend with the Spirit or without the Spirit, a few things being altered, as we shall say in its place. Now we shall set out the difference of the operations of Saturn and of his Angels according to the four principal quarters, with the conjurations appropriated to each in order; these are to be used when you announce a secret through the Spirit.

On the first Angel of Saturn, who is principal, and is called Orifiel, who observes the first quarter of Saturn.

[unclear]

The first and principal angel of Saturn, as we have said in the preceding sections, is called Orifiel; he, with the other angels of the planets in his order, rules the sphere for 354 years and four months. He has the first part both in the day and in the night; and through him the operation is performed from sunrise in the day, and from sunset in the night, up to the third hour inclusive, in all things that pertain to Saturn, and on his day and night, as we have said. Therefore, when in the first quarter of Saturn you wish to announce something to one absent without words and without letters, then no Spirit of Saturn other than Orifiel is to be summoned by you, because through him you will be able to announce everything most perfectly. First consider in what sign this Saturn is, and in what degree, and whether he is direct or retrograde, and with what planets he is in conjunction. Let us set down an example of the first point: Behold, Saturn is now in the 25th degree of Taurus, on the 28th day of the month of April in the present year, which is the year of the Lord 1500. Now therefore let us multiply 25, and they become 600; let us divide these by the four equal quarters, and there will remain to each quarter 150. Let us complete all the degrees of Saturn in the sign of Taurus, and there will be 30. But let us multiply 3 by 25 in all, and they become 750. Let us cast off the four superfluous degrees from the middle of the third quarter, and 650 will remain. Now let us take the point of Saturn’s motion from the table for the present day and hour; and we shall be able to know what is the rising, elevation, and setting of the Angel Orifiel with Saturn in the first quarter. Once these are known, our operation will be easy.

His diligentissime consideratis, Orificelem Saturni constat esse separatum à Saturno 25 gradibus, &amp; 15. minutis: est ad Orientem, à primo puncto motus Saturni 625. gradatio-nibus distans, à fine motus 25. minutis. His cognitis, fac imaginem ex cera, vel pingē in chartam nouam figuram Orifielis in modum viri barbati et amp; nudi, stantis super taurum varij coloris, habentis in dextra librum, &amp; in sinistra calamũ quem dum facis, dic: Fiat haec imago magni Orifielis plena, perfecta et amp; apta nunciare mentis meae secretem N. filio N. amico meo secure, fideli-ter et amp; integre, Amen. Scribe in fronte nomen tuum cum encausto ex oleo rosarum temperato, &amp; in pectore nomen amici tui abscentis diceens, Haec est imago N. filii N. cui per Angelum Saturni Orifielem nunciatur mentis meae conceptum, Amen. In fronte imaginis scribe Merion et amp; in pectore Troesda. Deinde coniunge ambas imagines simul, dicens: In nomine Patris et amp; Filij et amp; Spiritus sancti, Amen. Audi Orifiel princeps Stellae Saturni, &amp; per virtutum omnipotentis Dei adiuro te, auscultate: pręcipio et amp; mando tibi per virtutem istius imaginis tuae, vt nuncios N. filio N. hanc intentionem meam (explicetur intentio) quantocy-us secure, secrete et amp; fideliter, nihil obmittens eorum, quae eum volo scire, &amp; quae tibi commendaui. In nomine Patris et amp; Filijs et amp; Spiritus Sancti, Amen. Deinde inuolue ipsas imagines sic connectas simul panno loto cum aqua albi sine, &amp; pone eas in vas mobile, quod appellant sapientes Indix pharnat alronda: &amp; cooperi illud superius diligenter cum corio raso, ac pone in introitu alicuius habitationis claufra, vbicunque volueris, ad spaciũ 24. horarum: &amp; sine omni hesitatione tuum desiderium intra illas 24. horas perfecte adimpletur: scietaque amicus tuo us absens intentionem in omni forma perfectissime, sicut eam super imaginem dixeristi (quantumcunq̃ prolixa fuerit) &amp; quicquid illum ex te scire volueris, sciet in illis 24. horis perfecte et amp; secre-tissime: ita qđ nunquam in aeternum aliquis homo poterit hoc percipere aut scire sine voluntate tua aut amici tui. Et est magnum secretum, qđ nullus sapientum ante nos literis commendare ausus fuit. Tu autem, 24. horis elapsis, leua imagines de loco, in quo positae sunt: & repone eas, quia omni tempore Orifielis per eas operari potes non solum ad illum amicum tuũ, sed ad quoscunque alios, mutato duntaxat nomine ipsius amici in illius nomen, quem volueris aliquid scire. Et nota, quod non opportet ipsas imagines depingi pulchras aut curiosas: sed quan- tùm cunque simplices fuerint, nihil refert: modo habeant ali- quam similitudinem proportionatam, ita vt imagines hominũ esse cognoscantur. SECVNDVS Angelus Saturni vocatur Sadael, qui est primus sub Oriﬁele in ordine constitutus, &amp; habet secúdam partem post suum principem, tam in die quam in nocte, in operibus et amp; temporibus Saturni: hoc est quartam, quintam, &amp; sextam horas in aequales. Cum itaque in his tribus horis aliquid nunciare volueris ad a- micum absentem in viginti quatuor horis, sine literis, sine ver- bis et amp; sine nuncio: fac id per omnia et amp; signum, que in operatione praecedenti diximus: &amp; obserua punctum secundi motus Satur- ni in gradibus suis ad signum, in quo planeta ipse mouetur, & qualis fit motus, &amp; vbi sit Spiritus mouens astrum, quantum re- cesserit, &amp; quantum eleuetur à centro sui motus, quantum cun- que distet à puncto quolibet totius circuli siue sphaerae. Book Three.

When these things have been most diligently considered, it is clear that Orifiel of Saturn is separated from Saturn by 25 degrees and 15 minutes; he is toward the east, distant from the first point of Saturn’s motion by 625 gradations, and from the end of the motion by 25 minutes. When these things are known, make an image out of wax, or paint on new paper the figure of Orifiel in the likeness of a bearded and naked man, standing upon a bull of varied color, holding in his right hand a book, and in his left a reed-pen. While you are making it, say: Let this image of great Orifiel be full, perfect, and fit to announce the secret of my mind to N., son of N., my friend, securely, faithfully, and completely. Amen. Write on the forehead your own name with ink tempered with oil of roses, and on the breast the name of your absent friend, saying: This is the image of N., son of N., to whom through Orifiel, angel of Saturn, the conception of my mind is announced. Amen. On the forehead of the image write Merion, and on the breast Troesda. Then join both images together, saying: In the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. Amen. Hear, Orifiel, prince of the star of Saturn, and by the powers of almighty God I adjure you, listen: I command and order you, by the power of this image of yours, that you announce to N., son of N., this intention of mine (let the intention be explained) as quickly as possible, securely, secretly, and faithfully, omitting nothing of those things which I want him to know, and which I have entrusted to you. In the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. Amen. Then wrap those images, thus fastened together, in a cloth washed with water of white [wine?], and put them in a movable vessel, which the wise call Indix pharnat alronda; cover it carefully above with shaved leather, and put it in the entrance of some closed dwelling, wherever you wish, for the space of 24 hours; and without any hesitation your desire will be perfectly fulfilled within those 24 hours. And your absent friend will know your intention in every form most perfectly, just as you spoke it over the image, however long it may have been; and whatever you wish him to know from you, he will know within those 24 hours perfectly and most secretly, so that no man will ever be able to perceive or know this for all eternity without your will or that of your friend. And it is a great secret, which none of the wise before us dared to commit to writing. But that friend of yours, if he wishes you to know anything from his affairs, can make you more certain through the same spirit within the same space of 24 hours, provided he is well perfected in this art. But you, when 24 hours have elapsed, take the images from the place in which they were put, and put them away, because at every time of Orifiel you can operate through them not only for that friend of yours, but for any others whatsoever, merely changing the name of that friend into the name of the person whom you wish to know something. And note that the images themselves need not be painted beautiful or elaborate; however simple they may be, it makes no difference, provided they have some proportionate likeness, so that they are recognized as images of men. But if anyone wishes and is able to paint them beautifully, it will not hinder, nor does it help.

Concerning the second angel of Saturn, who is the first under Orifiel and is called Sadael, presiding over the second quarter of Saturn.

The second angel of Saturn is called Sadael, who is appointed first under Orifiel in order, and has the second part after his prince, both by day and by night, in the works and times of Saturn: that is, the fourth, fifth, and sixth unequal hours. Therefore, when in these three hours you wish to announce something to an absent friend within twenty-four hours, without letters, without words, and without a messenger, do it in all respects and by the sign which we stated in the preceding operation; and observe the point of the second motion of Saturn in its degrees toward the sign in which that planet itself is moved, and what the motion is like, and where the spirit moving the star is, how far it has receded, and how far it is elevated from the center of its motion, however far it is distant from any point of the whole circle or sphere. To attain knowledge of these things, this is the table.

When the place of the angel Sadael has been found from consideration of the fixed star at the point of Saturn’s motion, make two images, in the manner which we described in the preceding operation, of Orifiel, with the inscriptions, adjurations, and all the other individual things that were stated there. When these have been completed, place those images upon five little branches of the herb thrasnote, outside the house in a safe and secret place, and say over them:

In the name of the + Father and + the Son and + the Holy Spirit. Amen. Just as I have placed these two images of the angel Sadael and of N., son of N., my friend, joined together upon these five movable branches, so I command you, Sadael, by the power of Orifiel, your great prince, that without delay you convey to the knowledge of the aforesaid friend the secret of my mind which I have entrusted to you by explaining it.

When these words have been said, leave the images there for 24 hours; and what you wished will be done, and your friend will know, most perfectly and secretly, everything that you said over the images. Likewise, if you wish to know about someone absent, how he is faring, and his true condition within 24 hours, however far away he may be, you will be able to know it in this way.

And, with the constellation observed, through this art you will be able to know all things that are done in the world.

Concerning the third angel of Saturn, who is second under Orisiel and is called Pomiel, presiding over the third quarter of Saturn.

The third angel of Saturn is called Pomiel, who is second in order under Orisiel, the principal angel of Saturn. He presides over the seventh, eighth, and ninth Saturnine hours, both in the day and at night, in all matters that pertain to the operation of Saturn. Since he moves with his order among the fixed stars 25 degrees from the East, you will find his place, once his hours have been set out in tables, as follows.

Preface of Johannes Trithemius

It is the opinion of the wise that the ancient philosophers of art and nature, who had discovered secrets, concealed them by various methods and figures, so that they might not come to the knowledge of wicked men. The more learned among the Jews also confirm that Moses, the most famous leader of the Israelite people, in his description of the creation of heaven and earth, disclosed ineffable mysteries of secrets in simple words. Saint Jerome, most learned among our own, says that in the Apocalypse almost as many mysteries lie hidden as there are words. Moreover, the wise men of the Greeks, of no small esteem among their own people, who devoted their effort to writing fables, with most prudent reasoning handed down one thing to the unlearned and another to the wise in the course of a single narration. I cannot but admire these most zealous lovers of wisdom, and I do not fail to read them with whatever industry I can, so that, while I consider that they labored by lamplight more greatly than other men, I may, as best I can, fill the empty belly of my memory with certain crumbs, as it were, of knowledge falling from the table of the rich philosophers.

Nor, as I think, has this opinion altogether deceived me, since by the continual labor of reading I have learned many things that I did not know, and in various ways I have reserved an approach for my thoughts toward investigating greater secrets of things. Although, indeed, I am not of such great learning or industry that I would dare profess that I have grasped that secret method of the ancient sages which they used in concealing the majesty of philosophy, nevertheless I have devised certain methods, not to be despised, as it seems to me, of writing altogether secretly and without any suspicion, and of concealing whatever you wish. At the urging of the most serene prince, lord Philip, Count Palatine of the Rhine, Duke of Bavaria, and Prince-Elector of the Roman Empire, the wisest patron of philosophers, than whom no one seemed to me more worthy, I committed these methods to writing and gathered them into the following volume, not without enormous labor.

But lest this great secret come to the ears of the unlearned or of wicked men, whoever you may be as reader, I warn, ask, and adjure you by the ineffable name of God, JEHOVAH, and by the blood of our Lord Jesus Christ, savior of faithful souls, that you disclose this science of writing to no one unworthy, immodest, carnal, or maliciously old, since through it many things could be done among men: adulteries, fornications, conspiracies, murders, and betrayals, if, which may it not happen, it were made known. For just as a good and honorable man, as often as it is necessary, can safely and without any suspicion from anyone make known and express the secret of his will to another person who knows the art, for private or common advantage, so a perverse man, immodest and blinded by carnal love, can signify to a consenting person of his desire, however shamelessly, foully, and lustfully, his evil desire, by honorable, modest, and holy words, determining the place, time, and manner of meeting, as broadly as he can, without any suspicion. Nor will there henceforth be any security among married people, while a woman can very easily understand the evil will of her lover from the best writings, with her husband looking on and praising the most holy words, without any suspicion of evil; and whatever you wish your mistress to know, however ignorant she may be of Latin words, she can send back in reply, with her husband marveling and, as is possible, carrying the message. Indeed, if this science were to come to the knowledge of the commonwealth, the whole order would be disturbed, public trust would perish, letters, documents, all writings, and the very conversations of men would be turned into the gravest suspicion. No one now by letters, however

whenever thereafter no one would believe good, holy, and honorable men; no one would put trust in letters, however holy and chaste their words might be; it would always be thought that deceit, fraud, and evil deception lay hidden in the mouth, and men would become fearful about everything, no less suspicious of mutual conversations than of any letters whatever. But let someone object to me, saying: If you wanted this knowledge of yours to be hidden, why did you wish to commit it to writing? To him I say, if an answer must be given, that I neither ought nor could hide this knowledge from the most excellent prince, by means of which he may, if occasion arises, be able to free his dependants, of whose number I am one, from many dangers. For by means of this knowledge he can make known the conception of his mind to his own people, to whomever he wishes, secretly or openly, securely, without in the least fearing anyone's knowledge to the contrary. But whoever wishes to write anything by this art should diligently observe the methods, signs, and proportions of each thing; if he neglects to consider these, he himself will easily be able to forget what he has written. But now, with the Lord's help, let us proceed to the demonstration.

Method

The First Method of Writing Secretly is Carried Out by the Individual First Letters of Individual Words; Its Sign Is This: I.

The first, then, of the methods for writing secretly is such as this: when you wish to write something secretly to a friend, so that no one understands your intention except the one to whom you are writing, then take any Latin narrative you wish which need not be hidden, arranging all its words in such an order that the first letter of each word yields the word you wish, just as I shall teach you in the argument or example placed below. Yet this device is not sufficiently safe, because it could easily be detected by an industrious man, [unclear]. In reading, indeed, it is easy, but it is written with difficulty, because it is laborious always to have at hand words suitable to the proposition. Let us set down an example of this method, whose open text is Latin, but whose tenor, [unclear], is indicated as written in German, namely:

Precautions to Be Observed

But it must be observed that the aforesaid method, as we have said, is not sufficiently safe in serious matters, since as soon as any suspicion begins to arise about the letters, the secret can easily be detected by a clever person. Therefore the following methods are safer, as is clear. Likewise it must be observed, if by this or other methods you write to someone not sufficiently learned in the Latin language, that he should not divide the words, lest [unclear]. If you wish, you may use two points; I fill each word of your secret so that, when you have made a complete sentence of the outer text, you may make a little stroke thus, or the reverse, as you like. Yet it seems safer that neither points nor little strokes be made; and let the sign of a period, of whatever method, be placed not in the word of the secret, but rarely; place it neither over the first letter nor after the last, just as I did above in the hidden tenor: Dear fa[unclear]ithful one, etc.

Extension

Of Johannes Trithemius, Abbot of Sponheim

Extension of This First Method

The first method itself of writing secretly, like nearly all the others, can be varied with manifold diversity, so that a person who perfectly understands the aforesaid order of concealing may still be able to perceive only with difficulty other methods to be inferred from it. For anyone can vary this method, together with the others, for his own book: namely, so that the first line is conscious of the secret, the second not; or, if it is of such size, that one is not; and so consequently the concealer of secrets, as he wishes, is alternated in alternate lines, either whole or half, by descending from the beginning of his letters to the end, or by ascending from the end to the beginning. I add also that from either side, descending and ascending [unclear] another beside the sense of his hidden [unclear] can be varied by powers so many and so diverse that, in explaining them, there is need of an Oedipus. But my present purpose is to show first the simple methods of writing, and to give to those who are worthy and suitable to know many things an occasion by which they may be able elegantly to devise the greatest things from the smallest.

The Second Method, Prudently Varied by Alternate Words, Easy and Very Safe in Every Language

The second method of writing hidden things without suspicion is that the words of the narrative of the openly proposed text be varied by alternate position: namely, so that when the first letter of the first word bears witness to the hidden intention, the first letter of the following word is free from the duty of the secret office. Afterwards the third is not free from the ministry, the fourth remains idle, and so consequently the words, mixed always in alternate turns, serve the secret, while those suited to the public discourse withdraw in prudent order from the signification of hidden things. And this method, easy in every language of the world, contains [unclear] and seems to me sufficiently safe for announcing whatever secrets you wish. Its example is as follows.

The third method is to use alternate words in such a way that the first is always without the meaning of the secret.

The third method of secret writing, as I have said, arises from the preceding one; in it the words serving the secret are varied in alternate turns as above. Yet this must be observed: that the first word of the narrative contribute nothing to the secret intention; and, likewise, the last word of the completed sentence at the end should be without a word of the secret, together with the following word, which should precede the beginning of the next word. And this method is very safe and is not easily detected by one ignorant of the art; and we shall set down an example of this kind.

The fifth mode proceeds with the first null through two signifying ones; it concludes each thing with an alternate null.

The fifth mode, not very dissimilar to the fourth, proceeds in the customary way with the first null through two signifying words. Each word of the secret, containing one null, is always enclosed, if they are equal, by two signifying words and one null; but if the matter is among unequal ones, a solitary signifying word will stand between two nulls. Let us also set down an example of this kind.

The Sixth Method, after two nulls, always takes two significatives, whether they are words or are not.

The sixth method is that, with the first two being nulls to avoid suspicion, the two following in the order of the secret signify; and if by words of equal syllables they had completed the hidden word, that word itself is, in the usual way, closed off by two idle ones; if not, until the narration falls equally through two or more mysteries, where the nulls end some hidden word, presently what follows is begun from the significatives. Let us also offer an example of this mystery.
