The keys of the Steganography can all be varied with manifold diversity, according as it shall have seemed suitable to any diligent person for the concealment of his secret; but now let us set down below an example of this sort.

Seventh Example.

[unclear]

Unfailing light, blessedness of all the saints and creator [unclear], I.C. [unclear] of the universe and ruler, have mercy on us. We, weak, groaning, and thirsting for your mercy, ask you: grant us the strength to overcome the temptations of the Devil, so that, after hard labors for you, we may deserve rest. O sweetest Savior, I pray, look upon your humble servants and useless servants; be merciful to us, since we desire with all our longings to serve you. Make us have the favor of your love always burning within us. Give us the strong bond of brotherly charity. Jesus, almighty King of heaven, make us truly humble and vigorous despisers of worldly things, so that, always burning with love for you, we may love nothing here and regard nothing temporal as pleasant to us. O teacher of humility, most gentle Jesus, teach us to imitate your doctrine; for we are subject to various evils, intent on few goods. Save us, Lord, lest we perish. O supreme truth, give us life; sweet refuge of souls, be to us a tower of strength. For you are our strongest virtue; you are the salvation of my soul and the most healthful refreshment of my mind; you are the ineffable joy of the angels and the rest of all the faithful. You are the holy gladness of those who love you. You are the inextinguishable name of the citizens above. You are the giver of life to the dead and the most merciful sustainer of the frail. You, sweetest Jesus, help us, your frail servants, so that we may deserve to walk along the way of truth on the right path without offense. O most loving Lord Jesus, mitigate my very hard exile; and when the end of this life of mine begins to draw near, deign mercifully to come to our aid then, since [unclear], and fleeing far away all those who intend evils, they will soon be destroyed, since you are our protector. We ask by the virtue of your most noble death, sweetest one: do not despise your servants on the day of our departure, but may Jesus the Lord redeem and wash each of us with your blood, and may all [unclear] of our transgression graciously grant us, as we wait, the heavenly joys of the celestial homeland. Amen.

The eighth method proceeds alternately by three empty words and the same number of significant words.

As the sixth does by two, so namely that any single mystical word of equal syllables completes the meaning of the open narrative in such a way that, when three empty places have been left, the following one begins not from [unclear], but from three significant words. If the word of the secret has unequal syllables, it will receive [unclear] into its company, until the syllables before the period in some way at last become equal.

The ninth mode begins from three vacant ones, and proceeds singly through as many significants in alternating turns.

The ninth mode begins from three vacant ones with the eighth, and through as many significations alternately [unclear] concludes the individual mystical words before the period with an equal syllable, that is, it is concluded by three and three through as many idle ones; but the redundant ones, if two, are ended by two, and if one, by one similar vacant letter, in such a way, if you wish, that the following mystical word is always begun with three vacant ones. Of this let us set down the following example.

The ninth example.

Greeting and affection, most beloved and most singular friend, [bearer] of the present letters and more glorious, whom I ask you to receive humanely; he will set forth to you his necessity. Since I desire, as far as I can, to relieve here his old-time necessity and the defects pressing upon him, I should wish to be able to apply consolation to his misfortunes; but since, as is clearer than daylight to you, we are exhausted by heavy losses and, as is indicated, burdened by various debts, I am strongly confident in his zeal of piety, you who hold the force and bonds of friendship, that you would willingly show yourself humane to a friend, just as you have always been accustomed to be a helper of the needs of friends. And so I ask that you lend him, for a fixed term, two hundred florins, since he is placed in the greatest necessity, as he will inform you. I trust that you will restore all things with ready integrity after he has at last been moved by you. But if you do this, I give immortal thanks; act so that we may prove your sincere love toward us in the matter. What you do for him, I would have you know, is done for me; and I shall take care to give you immortal thanks for it. The friend himself, however, Eberhard, will restore it, namely

The tenth method begins by means of four nulls, proceeds, and ends with meaningful and idle letters.

The tenth method begins from four idle letters. Through the same number of signs in order it proceeds after the likeness of the eighth in threes; that is to say, when the mystic word ends in a vowel, what follows is begun from the meaningful letters; but if it ends in meaningful letters, that is incorporated from four idle letters. But if fewer than four letters remain around the end, it can be concluded with the same number of idle letters, and also be omitted in the same number of meaningful letters. Let us set down an example of the tenth.

S.D. Since it is useful to know how to adorn a most honorable talent, and since we judge nothing more shameful to befall men than ignorance. The vanity of the world is always hostile to good and excellent talents, since it swallows a noble intellect in filth, clouds the mind, scatters memory, disturbs the senses, overthrows discipline, weakens the body, effeminates the spirit, and makes the citadel of religion and piety into woodland tales out of a man; it consumes all time in vain things, seeks the comfort of the flesh, and transgresses into destruction all the brightness of Catholic instruction; it does not revere God, it despises men, it forgets benefits, it is disturbed by the evils of conscience, it rejects eternal joys and venerates human glory, it feeds on vices, it is stained with filth and every kind of foulness,

it thinks nothing of future things; stripped of eternal goods, it greedily loves only temporal things.

The eleventh method runs alternately through four, and concludes the word bound with meaningful letters by empty ones.

The eleventh method is always begun from four empty letters, and, proceeding alternately through the same number of meaningful letters, is ended in idle letters equal to the last meaningful letters. For all things to be concealed take their beginning from four idle letters, and however many meaningful letters you find remaining beyond four, know that so many empty letters must be appended at the end. Let an example of this be set down.

Example of the eleventh method.

S.D. I send you the oration that I delivered at the wedding of that same friend of mine: God, creator of all things, redeemer of the human race and best savior, consecrated even the use of marriage, lest the species itself perish. For we read that he also commanded marriage to the first man and said, Increase and multiply. He laid down the law for the preservation of humanity; and in the Gospel he deigned to sanctify weddings with miracles, those deserving well of God, preserving chastity. But it benefits men more who take up the modest zeal of their human state. Therefore you, who have taken up blessed wedlock according to our example and the command of the savior, who sometimes by miracles, but I by words, shall praise the institution of religion in honor of weddings. To you men, therefore, to whom we must announce weddings, and a great union of the young and religious [unclear]

Johannes Trithemius, Abbot of Sponheim

by which the human race is preserved: for if the practice of marriage had not existed, our whole race would have fallen and perished, with no one coming to its aid. But come, you who adorn fruitful marriages: let them be venerable by right conduct, by notable examples, by the concord of peace. First of all worship God, [unclear], always spend much money in alms for the poor, live virtuously, preserve justice, love beneficence, always speak praises to God, give alms from your own. Obey the commandments of God, do not abandon truth, honor the ministers of God, pay tithes to the churches, receive pilgrims as guests, free the innocent, feed the hungry, obey your elders, honorably love your neighbors, doing injury to absolutely no one; cultivate the Christian religion most devoutly; do not follow any vain errors that have been devised. Preserve the teaching of the Gospel, and live according to the commandments of God. Despise the pleasures of the flesh, show yourselves honorable and kindly, preserve purity of heart. Loving nothing [unclear]: remember what he commanded us in the holy Gospel, C. I., saying: [unclear] when at last we preserve chastity for God amid a voluptuous life and the soul in a muddy body. Purity of heart, however, must always be nourished by honorable, humble prayer, by which the mind is purified by prayers, and prayer most powerfully removes the remedy against temptations; and therefore the holy Apostle tells you that you must always be intent upon holy prayers, lest you fail through some temptation. Let us join you in marriage, so that, by his granting, you may preserve the offspring of your race, not so that you ought to flow away in harmful pleasures [unclear] the noble dignity of substance that is to come. And so know and keep in memory that you are travelers returning to the fatherland to which you have been called; for the life of this age is brief and quickly comes to an end. Therefore live in marriage in such a way that you do not at last happen to be excluded from the kingdom of God. Farewell.

The Hidden Tenor of the Aforesaid.

We have found a great secret treasure in the earth; come quickly and help lift it out. It is fully 100,000 guilders.

The twelfth method begins its narrative with five null letters, and, proceeding alternately through the same number of significant letters, joins them, just as in the tenth we showed that it must be done through four. Let us also devise the following example of this method.

Example XII.

S.D. I had lent you my book on the deeds of the Lombards, and the volume of Bede on the times; these I ask you to send back. For it befits a wise man to be [unclear] in those things which he has promised, [unclear] of the benefits [unclear]. The injustice of dealings is twofold, namely that of unworthiness and ingratitude. Lest you [unclear] yourself to be ungrateful, since you did not keep faith with what you promised, [unclear] you most gravely with the fault of levity. Our Gracius accuses you, because, though so often asked for the loan, you rashly refused to restore it to us according to the faith promised. Farewell.

The Hidden Tenor of the Aforesaid.

The Thirteenth Method.

It begins its narrative with five null letters and concludes the mystic word, through the same number of significant letters, [unclear] if they were of the same letter with the eleventh. Further, if there are fewer than five letters of the mystery, or if any remain after five, they must be concluded with as many null letters as the significant letters that immediately preceded them in number; but the mystic word, however many significant letters it has, is nevertheless begun from five null letters. Let us also devise the following example of this method.

Example XIII.

Johannes Trithemius, Abbot of Sponheim.

Princes have most wisely been accustomed not to shut up riches to be kept in treasuries, but to apply them to the use of letters, judging this the most honorable path for those tending toward happiness: the benefit of letters, by which the commonwealth is made immortal. For indeed the knowledge of writings from [unclear] is called the burial of the living. It brings ignominious calamity upon human beings and makes them like beasts; true nobility, by contrast, is accustomed to make the soul splendid with learning and virtues. Infinite is the fruit of letters, which wins glory and holiness for our souls in heaven and shows itself immortal to those born of earth. Add that love of writing, since it extinguishes the fires of the flesh, harmful to the spirit, alone conferred on those ancient philosophers the finest memory and immortality of name among all posterity, always enclosed as venerable to human beings. Philosophy also makes those devoted to the studies of the ancestors glorious and splendid, lovers of tranquility, just, gentle, conquerors of the passions of the soul, most steadfast despisers of luxury and baseness. For these there is an easy ascent to God; holy exercises are an example of honorableness and a rule for every virtue; it shines forth in contemplation of heavenly things, sweetly raised up. They attain divine illumination, dear to God in honor, reverenced by men. Imitate these things, devote yourself to letters, confirm the happiness of life by upright works. Farewell. I, Johannes Trithemius, abbot, have written this.

The hidden tenor of the foregoing.

Those of Nuremberg have sent scouts out against you / in many forms / look out for yourself / etc.

Mode XIV. Between two nulls it encloses each mystical word with its signifying words.

Mode 14 always takes its beginning from a null and, duly proceeding in order through signifying matter by means of one null, encloses at the end the word to be hidden. Moreover, students in this art will be able not only to vary but also to enlarge the preceding thirteen modes, so that, beginning with those things at the various number where we ended the demonstration, they may ascend, up to whatever number they wish, by 7, 8, 9, 10, or more alternately, wherever they wish.

Example

24 Key of Steganography. Example XIV.

Apply yourself to letters with humble submission; be kind; most diligently beware ignorance. For teaching, celebrated by training, exalted in honorableness, learning distinguished by morals, is to be preferred to all honors. Knowledge immersed in vices has little worth, but diligent learning always makes a noble life, marked by virtues and adorned with examples of learning; adorned innocence is given esteem, since heavenly honor must be preserved by holy actions. Unfruitful knowledge will be subject to torments, but in elevated sciences friendly letters [unclear] with living virtues, and pleasures that are stained and to be overthrown; one must insist on exercises of virtues, or sweetnesses must be granted. Farewell from Sponheim, 7 Kalends of January, in the year of Christ 1498. Johannes Trithemius.

The hidden tenor of the foregoing.

I ask you, let me know how the matter stands, as you well know.

Mode XV. It begins from the unit that marks, and proceeds alternately up to the number eight.

Mode 15 sets one idle word before, adds another signifying word, then two alternates, three follow, and so up to eight; moreover from the group of eight through seven, then through six, and so consequently down to the unit, the descent is again made; and again, in the same way, ascent and descent to the unit, as often as will be necessary.

Example XV.

Most illustrious Prince, with humble subjection, greeting. Princes must rightly be instructed in good disciplines and with virtues and learning, and should justly hold and knowingly govern the commonwealth. For the most glorious authority of leaders is to apply themselves at once to arms and letters: to destroy the enemy in war, and by the arts of letters to adorn the mind, and to rule with courage and wisdom together. God, the most excellent illuminator of all hearts, has bestowed noble knowledge upon us, which I shall, to the best of my powers, care for by your grace. God has given us the grace of understanding; he has set forth various arts not uselessly. But [unclear] to carry out the matter with zeal and to apply ourselves to holy impulses, so that we may deserve to enter the happiness of life appointed for us after death; and knowledge will be a support to us. The hidden content of the aforesaid.

I beg your Grace: keep the art secret until the book is made; I have found still wondrous things for it.

Mode XVI. It agrees with the preceding mode in its procedure, but, on the contrary, always begins from the vacant words.

The third mode is opposed to the preceding one as regards the beginning, because that one begins its first narrative from significant words. This one, however, begins from idle words, so that the first word is always empty, but the second significant; and so an ascent is made from unity up to the octave, from which again there is a descent down to unity, and this as often as the proposed narrative is finished. Let us fashion the following example of this kind.

Example XVI.

One ascends to eternal life by virtues alone, since those given over to vices have by no means been judged worthy of the kingdom of God, and their pride has been repelled; they are zealous for the iniquity of demons, and they will always be disturbed by zeal [unclear], and the worms of impiety will gnaw them. Their consciences will never rest for eternity, but, blinded, they will be punished with the greatest torments, with everlasting oblivion. In hell there is no redemption, but perpetual weeping and unceasing groaning and a fire never to be extinguished. There are darkness and everlasting night, fear and very grievous misery, cold and chill; there will be no degree, for always to lack perpetual goods, to endure burning or cold or [zeal?], which is blameworthy. For carnal pleasure is very brief; in exchange for its object, wretched men are increased by the greatest miseries, [unclear]; but the salvation of our people remains continually [unclear]. Farewell.

The hidden content of the aforesaid.

When this man comes to you, put him in prison until my arrival, etc. And so with the rest as much as one pleases.

Mode XVII. It imitates the first mode through the individual words, the letters always being in the preceding one.

The seventeenth mode, after the pattern of the first, begins with the first letters through the individual words, but arranges the letters of the alphabet artfully, so that for a it takes b, for b it takes c, and so consequently up to the end of the alphabet; moreover, for z it takes A. And when you wish to write in such a mode, so that you may the more easily be able to follow the alphabet, consider its order by nature.

A b c d e f g h k l m n o p q r s t u x z.

b c d e f g h i k l m n o p q R S T U X Z A.

For A, b, the immediately following letter, is taken; for B, C; for D, D [unclear]; and so consequently, as is clear in the example.

30. Key of Steganography. Method XXI. It uses alternating significant words, with the letters transposed into the second place.

Method 21 uses alternating words, of which the first is empty, the second indeed significant, the third again empty, the fourth by no means idle; and so on in succession down to the end of the proposed narrative. All the letters in the significant word are transposed into the second following place, so that for the letter A, c is to be taken; for c, e is to be taken; and so on in succession to the end of the alphabet. Further, for x, a is to be taken, but for z, b. The Greek y, however, is not necessary for us for an ordinary name, and therefore is to be omitted in all the following alphabets. But now let us set down an example of this kind.

Example XXI.

I should rejoice to answer your letters; so may Christ make me rejoice, and I would send the requested volumes, if at last I had had them. I have been zealous, I think, for my nearest and most serious hidden handlers lately with a good zeal, as the most exact philosophers had it; moreover I shall have for you thanks far from mortal, my sweetest brother, you who keep mutual glory inviolate. For in this familiar matter, which you seem to have attended to most diligently with grave modesty, I have plainly learned this: that I praise what has been done and shall have thanks that will never die. And therefore, complying with your requests, I should soon have wished to be, Christ knows, the things requested, if I had them. Here I have nowhere seen a Latin translation of Master Ficino; I confess I have read at Venice the beloved letter of Pico della Mirandola. Therefore do not take it hard that your petitions are so frustrated. The highest truth of your Christ conceals nothing in darkness, and, as examiner of hearts, that I could not oblige you. To hide the other best things, to scorn virtue and very many gains swiftly, at last you think true, to love Christ purely. I ask, see to it that you exist as a priest in works, and that the lover of Christ more truly love Christ purely, whom you are commanded to fear. He is preserved by zeal for souls, and sets nothing before Christ's commands, since he knows that the fear of God is the best zeal of the soul, the love of blessedness, God zealous by loving. For the true royal knowledge of the Savior, and the pious observance of the catholic faith, and increasing thanks to almighty God Jesus Christ, the more glorious giver of all good things, may confer on you loves of eternity, and inscribe you in the catalogue of faithful Christians. Farewell.

Tenor [unclear]

Johannes Trithemius, Abbot of Sponheim

31

The hidden tenor of the aforesaid.

Peter, printer of Fridburg, called Labsodel, likes to drink strong wine. He has been made Doctor of Fools at Sponheim.

Method XXII. With the transposition of letters already mentioned preserved, after two idle words he sets down the same number of significant ones.

Method 22 begins with idle things and at once adds two significant ones, and so, by means of two empty words and two significant words, it completes the whole open and hidden narrative in alternating turns. The first letters of all the significant words are placed in the third position, so that for a, d is to be taken; for b, e is to be taken; but for c, f; and so on in succession to the end, just as for the first letter of the alphabet A, x is to be taken; for b, [unclear]; and for z, c, as in secret matters the alphabet showing [unclear] their red visited black, hidden this time.

A d b c e f g h i k l m k p q r s x t z n a x ss z c.

But when you wish to write in the prescribed manner that follows, set the alphabet before you, and look carefully that you keep the prescribed order, lest you cause error for the reader and for yourself. But now let us set down an example, which proceeds by two alternating words.

Example XXII.

S D. Since I have known you to be a lover of the arts of humanity and of the devoted, and a cultivator of the Christian faith and the most benevolent patron of all philosophers, willingly, led by the wonderful pleasure of friendship, to oblige your requests, from books well known about ecclesiastical writers and catholic doctors, [unclear] for you to be exhorted, behold, I send it, so that you may have something with which to offend the mind. May you send back to me the codex from torments into books of foolishness concerning spirits, and the glorious work of [unclear] coming, which you have shuddered at in questions. I beseech Christ to adorn the eyes of our heart with the most holy zeal of his love, and to make us, freed from love of heavenly goods and from lowest desires, [unclear] to despise vain honors, so that in turn the lofty and also great secrets of the art may penetrate

32 Key of Steganography

that we may penetrate [unclear], and [unclear] a continual desire for glory, with the duty purified, whereby we may always adorn the Catholic faith with most honorable morals; by the virtue of humility may we become better every day, despise transitory things, and not seek to please men. You are a great and truer philosopher: let go of all things and you will find all things; and the discovery nearest to death, insofar as it offends the erring man. Farewell.

The hidden tenor of the aforesaid.

What I have given you to keep, you shall preserve and give to no one except to me alone.

Mode XXIII. With each letter shifted to the fourth, it proceeds by alternating turns or words.

Mode 23 always begins with one idle word, to which it immediately joins one significant word, and so proceeds with alternating words. In the meaning of these, the first letters are always transposed to the fourth, so that for a, e is taken; for b, f; for c, g; and so consequently as far as x, for which c is taken, as in the following alphabet we shall clearly show by example.

A e, b f, c g, d h, e i, s k, h l, i k, o l, p m, q n, r o, s p, d q, u l, r x, s z, t a, s b, x c, z d.

This mode, however, like all the others, will be capable of being varied in many ways: as it now uses alternate words, so let it use pairs, threes, or more. Then the sign of a mode of this kind is to be sought; and it must always be observed immovably for the others, since one should look not to the variety of the mode but to the order of the mystery.

Example XXIII.

S. D. Those matters which I set before myself to be solved, with Christ’s help I have resolved. I would like you to write back to me briefly what you make of it, what then has benefited me, your opinion, and the whole matter. Brother Gratius, and also a friend, recently reported to me that then, among our people, a young man had been restored to life, recounting every invocation of Christ from the dead, and telling of the wondrous and dreadful torments among the lower regions of wicked Christians: namely, of those who, by acting perversely, crucified Christ; those especially guilty who, though they had obtained the most kindly benefit of redemption, nevertheless always remained ungrateful to Christ and, utterly blinded, neglected future joys. Following the pleasures of the world, they were most bitterly [unclear] with daily and continual neglects gnawing at them: “We shall be condemned; we are justly tortured; deservedly do we suffer cruel things. Cruel as we are, we sought earthly and worldly things ambitiously; we neglected Christ’s commandment; we despised the humble; we loved iniquity; and we receive the repayment of eternal damnation. Alas for us unhappy ones, why did we deny Christ, why did we neglect the time of indulgence?” etc. The man raised up related that he had found many other wondrous things, etc. I cannot write them on this occasion, especially in a few letters. Farewell.

The hidden tenor of the aforesaid.

Tomorrow at nine o’clock take heed of me at the gate. There I will appear secretly and silently with 200 horses.

Mode XXIV. It takes all significant words, and transposes each letter to the fifth following.

Mode 24, after the likeness of the first, takes all the words of the proposed narrative as significant; but it transposes the first letter of each word to the fifth next following: that is to say, so that for a, f is taken; for b, g; for c, h; and so consequently, as we shall show in the second alphabet, where for the red letter the black one immediately placed above it is taken.

A f, b g, c h, d i, e k, f l, g m, h n, i o, k p, l q, r u, x z, s t, b v, c x, d z, e [unclear].

Therefore, whenever you wish to write or read in this mode, place this alphabet before you, easily indicating all the signs of each mode.

Example XXIV.

S. D. Setting the honor of benefactions before attentive services, and not provoking the insults of benefactors, remember, I beseech you, the holy charity of your brothers, the good zeal and honor of those brothers of yours who continually adorn our Catholic religion with holy works. But I pray, kind brother, that I may cast away fear. Double-tongued brothers, the hatred of being loved, quarrels, and disputes take goodness away by evil works. Be splendid every day to the good also; aspire also to fame; adorn the soul with holiness, justice, continence; and have zeal for the name [unclear].

The hidden tenor of the foregoing.

Do not heed my word; I do not mean it so harshly; it must now be so; I will tell you the reason.

Mode XXV. Like the preceding, it admits all significant words, but transposes each to the sixth.

Mode 25, like the preceding, admits no empty word, but all the words which it admits are significant, because there is no need to insert any idle words, since there is no one in this world who, without the art of this book, could discover the secret knowledge written in these modes. Nevertheless, whoever, for greater caution or for ease, wishes to insert alternately, or after two or more empty words, the same number of significant words, we do not forbid it, especially since we know the letter for each person, so that he may, at his own pleasure, either invent new ones, if he can, or alter these as he wishes. Yet we advise them not to neglect to put the signs of the modes in their proper place, lest he himself cause others to err, as we have done, if he writes in this mode; because in each one, and in this twenty-fifth, the letters are transposed to the following sixth, as we shall show in its place. There follow the twenty-five modes of the alphabet mentioned above, in which for A let g be taken, because it is the sixth after a; for b, c; i, d; k, e; l, f; m, g; n, h; o, i; p, k; q, t; r, m; s, n; t, o; u, p; x, q; z, r; a, s; b, t; c, a; d, x; e, z; f.

When, therefore, you wish to write something either in this mode or in the other modes, once the alphabet arranged for this purpose has been set before you, put the first significant letters, written on one sheet, before you, as we do below for an example.

Example

Of Johannes Trithemius, Abbot of Sponheim

Example of the hidden secret.

Keep all letters that I send you secret, and let no one see them. Now let us fashion a narrative for this hidden message.

Example XXV.

S D The humble, desiring grace with laments, obtain forgiveness; by the grace of redemption freedom is restored. But penitent men are mercifully set free. The precepts, the justification of piety by the most gracious giver of freedom, and all the things of the Catholic law, the most pious Savior, King of power, about to judge, has bestowed. To all who devoutly hold Catholic rectitude he has promised the joy of blessedness. Good power of freedom: those holding the holy law will rejoice at last as Catholics; they will kiss the most gracious liberator in tranquil light. Farewell, from Sponheim, 3 Nones of January, in the year of the Lord 1498. Jo. Trith., Abbot.

Mode XXVI. It proceeds by alternate words, and each letter of the significant words is transferred to the second.

Mode 26 proceeds by alternates like the second, first placing one empty word at the beginning, then another significant word, and so on successively to the end of the narrative. Moreover, for each first letter of the significant words, the seventh afterward in order is to be taken, namely: for A, h is taken; for b, i; for c, k; and so on in succession, as will be clear in the following alphabet, where the black letters are taken for the red.

Red. black.

A h b i c k d l e m f u g o b p i q k y l s m t n u o x p z q r r b s e t d u e x f z g.

But so that you may easily understand the art, and know the method of composing a common narrative for a secret message, I shall now set down and show you the customary knowledge in its own letters according to the seventh transposition.

When you wish to write in this mode the letters of empty words, as I have said—

Example XXVI.

S.P. I had entrusted my books to you under the condition of returning them, my very dear [unclear], but see, you have by no means returned them. You ought to have sent them back shortly; you act contrary to the law which the catholic faith has sanctioned concerning a promise. Do not disdain the condition longer than you promised. It does not befit a good and honorable man, sprung from a noble ancestry of elders, to violate a promise. You had promised to return them very diligently in a short time; it is a mark of levity to put off a promise every day to the Greek Kalends. Have I not waited long enough with great goodwill? It is disgraceful to promise great things and repay very small ones. A promise adorns a soldier, nor does it befit a Christian not to keep a condition. But the law and constitution, Christian, bid you keep promises, repay a loan, and do generously in turn to others the things which you desire to be done to you. I demand back my books, which I had entrusted to you with entreaties. I do not desire a longer excuse, which I stretch out to the Greek Kalends. Release my mind in brief. You possess the nobility of your most honorable family, Bunnesind; consider your lineage, and send my volumes back to me. Farewell.

The hidden tenor of the above:

This man wants to catch you badly; beware of him; he is full of wickedness and wants to test you. This is the intention of the secret.

Method XXVII. It uses alternate words, and each letter of the significant words is transferred to the following eighth letter.

Method 27. After one vacant word has been placed first, it immediately sets down another as significant, and so proceeds thereafter by alternate turns. But it transfers the first letter of each significant word to the eighth afterward, to the next following, so that for the letter A it takes I, for B K, for C L, and so on, as the alphabet written below shows more clearly.

To express the consequence of this sort of alphabet, let us set down an example, so that the words of the secret change the letters, the first letters of the significant words; afterward, the example.

The intention of the secret:

I wanted you to let me know how the matter stands with the money, and other things besides, as you know.

Example XXVII.

S.D. A rumor has gone out concerning the abbot of Limburg, that he has dismissed the brother of [Fleisderfensem?], a faithful man and experienced in temporal affairs, and has introduced new monks, lacking resources and assigning themselves to that office. I am greatly astonished at the counsels of the brothers; nevertheless, when I recall the custom of the Limburgers, I do not know what to say. For they are ignorant of temporal affairs, and therefore they dismissed a most faithful man when their saint reproved them. They ought to have said thanks to our Savior Jesus Christ for the faithfulness of so great a brother, who could have recovered their necessities. Wretched men, why do you reject a good and necessary administrator? What shall I say? I do not praise the departure of so useful a brother, most skilled in temporal affairs; he would have aided the Limburgers most quickly, which I deeply grieve, that the Limburg monks have been so foolish: they dismissed an excellent man and appointed as stewards monks worth absolutely nothing in temporal affairs. Abbot Macharius, it did not befit a man to act thus: at first you praised him, now you drive away a far better man, to be placed after no one. For I confess that if Christ had given him to me, I would give him the greatest thanks, as befits a Christian, and would see to it that he did not depart, [unclear] Christ. You preferred, having lingered, to dismiss a faithful man, worn out by the depravity of false men, lest I should seem, your affairs having been abandoned, [unclear] hope of recovering. Farewell. From Sponheim. Nones of January, in the year of the Lord 1499. Johannes Trithemius, Abbot.

Mode XXVIII. Like the preceding one, it uses alternate words, and transfers the signifying letter to the ninth.

Mode 28, like the preceding one, uses alternate words, of which the first is empty, the second signifying, the third again empty, the fourth signifying, and so on in succession. It transfers each letter to the ninth following, so that for A, k is taken; for b, l; for c, m; and so on, as will appear in the secret alphabet. But it must be known that this mode is varied in many ways, as are all the others; but when you wish to give something of this art to be read, for admiration, to someone who does not know the matter, take care [unclear] the individual signifying [words], but [unclear], because the alphabet is safer.

Dear Guardian, these two brothers have conducted themselves very Christianly in words and deeds.

Example XXVIII.

S.D. Reverend and venerable father, I know that you gladly grant to friends all things desired; therefore I humbly beseech you that, in view of Catholic piety, you do not [unclear] your brothers Zelesor, detained for a rather long time among us with the greatest charity; for they had to remain at my entreaty. It was a glorious joy for us; rejoicing not idly, but most devoutly, we exulted in devout joy, with special zeal for God and for the good of the Apostolic [unclear], giving thanks. Our joy was most devout; our gladness also adorned with most holy morals of every kind. The religious and Catholic brother beautifully adorned our gladness with the most holy zeal of discipline. For we exulted without dissolution of mind, always preserving ourselves most religiously. He was to all of us vigorously devoted and very like in prayer, adorned by reason of divine [unclear] and of the Church and of souls, by whose piety he was adorned; for us he furnished every theme and matter for disputation, approaching fervently and vehemently with most holy devotion of mind in the religion of piety. What, I beseech you, [unclear] a religious assembly, where Catholic conversation flourishes, where nothing idle is said, nothing hidden and wicked. May Christ Jesus, savior of all, make us rejoice in heavenly glory, and may the love and fervor of God refresh all true zealots of truth. We have rejoiced with holy joy, praying and entreating that you receive the brother peacefully and lay aside every zeal of bitterness. Farewell, from Sponheim, on the Nones of January, in the year 1598. Johannes Trithemius, Abbot.

Mode XXIX. It uses alternate words, and the first letter of each signifying word is transferred to the tenth.

Mode 29 likewise uses alternate words, as the preceding ones do, beginning with one empty word, to which another signifying word is immediately joined; again one empty word, and again one signifying word, and so on in succession to the end of the proposed narrative. But the first letter of each signifying word is transferred to the eleventh following, so that for A, l is taken; for b, m; for c, n; and so on, as appears in the alphabet itself.

A, b, m, c, n, a o, e p, f q g r h i k u x z na ob pc qd re ss g t g u h xi zk.

Tenor of the Secret.

Beware of the bearer of this letter; he is a wicked knave. Do not trust him at all; he is deceiving you. I know him very well.

Signifying Letters.

a man of much knowledge, a supreme philosopher, a most subtle arithmetician, a most eloquent rhetor, a most profound mathematician, and excellently learned in [unclear]. He speaks most elegantly, shining with Ciceronian eloquence. Were I not so great a friend to you, I would have kept the man entirely for myself, since, having been on familiar terms with him, I have found him to be the most learned of philosophers. I favor you especially, so receive gratefully so great a philosopher, whom, moved by singular friendship toward you, I send to you; and by showing yourself benevolent and familiar to him, you will find him a supreme philosopher. I have seen certain secrets of the arts committed to most elegant letters, by which [unclear] wonderful things. This most learned man can answer ex tempore the gravest questions put to him; in setting forth he uses a very ready zeal for disputation. I ask that you receive him generously and courteously, a man most learned in the culture and familiarity of all good arts and a most weighty defender. Indeed he will be able to instruct you in many things, since he is a philosopher of most elegant learning, an outstanding historian, a most skilled and ready rhetor, and also a very acute geometer. Would that all our students were such, who with swollen breast despise necessary study. But this man, devoted to philosophy, profoundly loves the other sciences and arts, treats them continually, and penetrates them most acutely. Receive him, therefore, with love; treat him with a generous countenance; strengthen a faithful Christian. Farewell from Sponheim, on the Nones of January, in the year of the Lord 1499. Johannes Trithemius.

Mode XXX. It proceeds by alternate words, and the significant letter is transferred to the eleventh.

Mode 30, beginning from one vacant word, proceeds through alternate words, so that throughout the whole sequence of the narrative it always places, after one vacant word, another significant one, as we have also shown in the preceding mode and in others. Further, by the fourth letter of the significant word, the eleventh following after it is to be taken, so that for A, m is taken; for b, n; for c, o; and so consequently, as is clear in the alphabet.

Am, bn, co, dp, eq, fr, gs, ht, iu, kx, lz, ma, nb, oc, pd, qe, rf, sg, th, ui, xk, zl.

Content of the Secret.

They have written to me that I should come to him; but I will not come unless you write to me beforehand.

Example XXX.

S. D. I send you a prayer concerning [the mother?], Mary ever Virgin, as you recently requested: [unclear] most loving, kindly mother, nourishing Mary, virgin, most radiant parent. You also most pleasing to the highest unity; you, most faithful helper of all who invoke you; you, noble refuge of those seeking you. For daily [unclear] of holiness; save [us], most gentle advocate of the poor, consoler of those who groan, most beautiful storehouse of virtues, most adorned. Hail, most kindly comforter of the sorrowful, and most celebrated promoter of the faithful friends of Christ. Rejoice, [Anna?], solace of those who mourn; rejoice, summit of nobility and sure hope of the faithful who labor. Obtain pardon for us who ask; [mitigate?] the dread Judge of Christianity. Help those contrite in heart; take away our souls, we beg; sanctify [us] by your goodness. Blessed are you, most honorable virgin mother, who bore in complete integrity, and as virgin gave birth to the almighty Savior, the Son of God, yet always remaining also a most pure virgin. The messenger Gabriel greeted her as full of grace, mother in humanity. Hail, mother, or inexhaustible fountain of indulgence in piety, shining with piety, most reverend to all by the very great magnitude of your benefits. Intercede for your servants; adorn us with your virtues, that we may attain blessedness after the end of this life by the kindness of the Savior of all the faithful. And may he who by his blood gave life to us wretched ones, with you interceding, receive [us] piously in his kindness [when dead?]. Amen. Farewell. From Sponheim, the seventh day before the Ides of January, in the year of the Lord 1499. Joh. Trith., Abbot.

Content of the Secret.

The old abbot of Fleissdorff wants to cut off the nose of the man from Reinhartsborn. This is the intention of the following mystery.

Signifying letters.

Example XXXI.

S. D. Everyone who, with regard to temporal things, gives alms [unclear] by virtues, and before a transitory thing no one can be a lover of justice, since true charity divides [unclear] under no condition. Finally, holy religion, the Christian faith, forbids love of the world to its people, because he who loves worldly joys loses eternal happiness; a Catholic who does not live in Catholic fashion does not love Christ.

And he who loves temporal things is not said to be a good Catholic; he who loves the Creator rejoices in spiritual things. A lover of Christ despises all the vanities of the world, and does not care for the joys of wicked men. A lover of the world hates holy virtues; he cares nothing at all for the joys to come. [unclear] Christ [unclear] not the thought intent upon one thing which are not honorable. Do not, wretched men, I beseech you, do not do things contrary to religion; do not love the vanities of this world, soon to perish. Rather take care to love Christ, so that he may receive you into the heavenly kingdoms. Farewell. From Spanheim, 7 Ides of January, in the year 1499. Johannes Trithemius, abbot.

Mode XXXII. It proceeds by alternating turns, and the first letter of the signifying word is transferred into the thirteenth.

Mode

Of Johannes Trithemius, Abbot of Spanheim.

34

Mode 32 is used in alternating divisions in the manner of the preceding ones; the narration of the mystery also begins from one empty division, to which it always joins in turn one signifying division. For the letter a, the first signifying division takes the thirteenth following after it in the order of the alphabet: for A, o is taken; for b, p; for c, q; and so consequently, as is clear.

A.o. h.p. c q. d r. e.f. f t. g.u. h.x. i z. k.a. l.b. m.c. n.d. o e. p f. q g. r h. s i. t k. ul. x m. z n.

Tonight still about 9 o'clock, when you hear me whistling by the wood with a key, then come down to me. This intention lies hidden secretly in the following narration.

Signifying letters.

De q x s z d k l o p 9 l x h l j dr l c z q xo dr sello brx ehf ik ft s Z tt s dc Zk sz d sciq xb lii sbie a ex s hop nlczh.

Example XXXII.

S. D. Almighty God, eternal creator of all things, who through your Son Christ redeemed us Christians, gave the zeal of love to Catholics through the light of grace, instilling piety in us who believe, and most generously gave your beloved Son as a man; free all of us believers from prisons, mourning under the power of the Tartarean one, destroying the most dark prison and conquering the [unclear].

What, O Christ, shall we Christians, weak men without works of justice, be able worthily to render to you? Professing the Catholic faith, therefore, most devoutly, we celebrate you, our redeemer, with the highest praises, saying: Praise be to you, eternal, most gracious savior of all, who redeemed us by your blood. Strengthen our frailty with the zeal of your love; save us, sweetest savior Jesus, and pour the zeal of faith into our hearts. Holy is your zeal; illumine with compunction for works the hearts of those who seek you, most gracious Christ Jesus. Most gracious Christ Jesus, eternal light, illumine the darkness of your servants with your accustomed goodness. Savior Jesus, save our souls, bestowing eternal joys. Christ, hear your humble servants, and pardon the sins of all who pray; save your Christian servants, though most unworthy; seal us with your zeal, we humbly ask. Amen. Farewell from Spanheim, 6 Ides of January, in the year of the Lord 1499. Joh. Trith.

Key of Steganography. Method XXXIII. Proceeding by alternate words like the preceding methods, it shifts the first significant letter to the fourteenth.

Method 33 begins the second narration with one idle word, and, like the preceding method, proceeds in turn by alternate words. For the first letter of each significant word it takes the letter following it in the fourteenth place, so that for A, p is taken; for b, q; for c, r; and so on according to the order of the following alphabet.

Alphabet. A-p, b-q, c-r, d-[s?], e-t, f-u, g-x, [unclear], i-a, k-b, l-c, m-d, n-e, [unclear], p-g, [unclear], r-i, s-k, [unclear], u-m, x-n, [unclear].

Tenor of the Secret. He is still new; test him first quite thoroughly before much is entrusted to him. He also likes to drink wine and is strange. This is the meaning of this secret.

Significant letters. Toaklefrzetmmmtikmrzazemfixpelommfctztsteazdmatomtilipmltiliaerblp mrzxtiemmstaemesakl mmfe carz

Example XXXIII.

Johannes Trithemius, to the holy nuns on the mountain once of Rupert, who adorn the Catholic faith with bright virginity: happiness. With continual zeal for most holy religion, for the sake of the aforementioned greatest king, we send a servant, requested by us for a long time, a great man, a man [unclear] in temporal matters. Johannes, known to your charities, zealous with fervor for the religion of the monastery of [Uleidorf?], for a long time abbot, and freely leaving a new abbacy, I approached therefore, just as I had committed to you the monastery of Limpurg, in which he served Christ, occupied with continual prayers and holy readings of the Scriptures, when he went down with the monks of the same place and took up the care of temporal affairs, and became procurator and cellarer. The abbot of Limpurg, changed in mind by his usual instability, finally consents to leave. I begged with the greatest urgency, and scarcely could obtain consent from him. Christ willing, he at last consents, though timidly, because he fears to serve nuns, since they are lightly changed. He fears not undeservedly; for, as experience has taught us, some nuns have given their stewards, for their beneficence, a reward not praiseworthy. A woman’s mind is suddenly changed to bitterness. Yet, Christ granting it, I trust that he will be useful to you. [unclear] Therefore, recognizing womanly changeableness, I admonish you to remember to be constant, receiving him in holy honor and sincere charity, putting aside every levity of womanly mind. Especially help us and recover the state of temporal affairs, collapsed in your monastery. It would be of benefit, with Christ our redeemer, the zealous lover of chastity, helping. Farewell, 7 Ides. Johannes Trithemius.

Of Johannes Trithemius, Abbot of Spanheim.

Method XXXIV. It similarly uses alternate words and shifts the first letter of each significant word to the fifteenth.

Method 34, like the preceding methods, begins with one idle word and proceeds similarly by alternate words, so that the first is idle, the second significant, the third again idle, the fourth in turn significant, and so on successively to the end of the proposed narration. Further, for the first letter of each significant word there is taken the letter which, in the following alphabetical order, comes after it in the fifteenth place, so that for A, q is taken; for b, r; for c, s; and so on, as is clear in the alphabet that follows.

Alphabet. A-q, b-r, c-s, d-t, e-u, f-x, g-z, h-a, i-b, k-c, l-d, m-e, n-f, o-g, p-h, q-i, r-k, s-l, t-m, u-n, x-o, z-p.

Hidden tenor. Tomorrow at 9 the bailiff will come and take the peasants’ cows; keep yours at home.

Significant letters. Eg kzuufuerfunfunkttukgehmeqfgceeufrutinfrqnkef thuenafueufrnahdwstubfatqa hue.

48 Key of Steganography

... it uses [unclear], and the first [letter] of each meaningful word is changed into the seventeenth following after it, so that for A, s is taken, for b, t, for c, u, and so on in succession to the end of the proposed narrative, as in the following alphabet.

Alphabet. A s, b t, c u, d x, e z, f a, g b, h c, i d, k e, l f, m g, n h, o i, p k, q l, r m, s n, t o, u p, x q, z r.

Content of the Secret. Priest Heintz of Mandel has carried off one from St. Catherine's; if you find him, then take him captive.

This is the meaning of the following mystery. Kasac zgdorpih gshxxfcsxzdhzpihnufocsmdhx spihbze pcmoadhzznopdohnihdedchbzafshbz̄h.

Example 36. Catholic faith does not save [unless] it is supported by the ardor of the divine name. Believe also that zeal for the love of God is by no means entirely useless here for the redemption of the soul, for many people are now found boasting in the Catholic faith, but few are performing the works of the Christian faith. Without works faith dies; they believe a great deal, but very few observe God's commandments. O weak zeal of faith, which stronger unbelieving men could have by natural uprightness; the Gentiles who do not believe that the Savior of the world was made the Son of God and made man through zeal for human redemption will be tormented by the pains of hell. But they do not in the least adorn the Christian faith with most holy works, and, always entangled in sin, put [unclear] honors before eternal blessedness, staining the purity of faith with impious actions and depraved morals against obedience. But the lovers of God who have the right zeal of the Christian faith, setting nothing before Christ, will have him as an appeased judge, and he will give them everlasting honor. [Unclear], therefore, from these discourses, you who boast of faith: love God and you will have the reward of blessedness of those who are zealous for righteousness. If you love the vanity of the world against the honor of God, you will receive the reward of those who are zealous for iniquity: the horrors of hell. Johannes Trithemius wrote this on the fourth day before the Ides of January, in the year 1500.

Mode XXXVIII. It uses alternating words in turn, and the first letter of the significant word is transferred to the 19th.

Mode XXXIX. It also uses alternating words, and the first letter of the significant word is transferred to the 20th.

Mode 39 uses alternating words in turn, beginning from one vacant word, or after a preceding vacant one it appends one significant word, then again one vacant word and again a significant word, and so consecutively up to the end of the proposition. Furthermore, the first letter of each significant word is transposed to the 20th next following, so that for A, x is taken; for b, z; for c, a; and so consecutively, as is clear in the alphabet itself.

Method XL. It uses alternate words, and transfers each first significant letter into the twenty-first.

Method 40, like the preceding ones, uses alternate words, empty and significant in the same place. The first letter of each significant word is transferred in order into the twenty-first, the next nearest following, which is the last of ours, so that for A, z is taken; for b, a; for c, b; and so consequently, as is clear in the alphabet of this fortieth method, which follows below. This method, however, like all the others, is varied into diverse other forms, so that it may use either single significant words, or alternate ones, or several.

Example LX.

[unclear]

Do penance, wretched people. Now, in a short time, you hardened ones will suffer the most grievous tribulations of our race from infidel men, and a most cruel death. The Turk, with a great army from Hungary, has attacked Christendom far and wide. Savage as beasts, the Turkish men [unclear] crossed the Danube, kindled as if by fire with zeal for impiety. Therefore let all men mourn, as those soon to die. Where is your zeal, most wretched Christians? Where your constancy and devotion? Far away, through wickedness, Christian kindness has [unclear]; [unclear] has abandoned the Catholic faith. Zeal and the fervor of divine love have gone far away; because of these things the enemies of the faith will kill and devour men like locusts. For we have heard how grievously the Turk, having invaded Hungary, Bohemia, and Poland, destroyed cities, and most shamefully violated infants, women, and gathered virgins, and consecrated women who out of zeal for God had preserved chastity, and horribly killed all Catholics whatsoever. Destroying all, his cruelty surpasses men and beasts. He will suddenly throw all Germany into disorder with his most warlike army unless a general defense of the princes resists without delay. Therefore, weeping, let us humble ourselves with the greatest contrition of souls, praying to God most earnestly that he convert us, mercifully forgiving [our sins?], freeing us from enemies who strive to hand our souls over to death. In the year of the Lord 1499, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of March.

Johannes Trithemius, Abbot of Sponheim.

54 Key of Steganography

Chapter II

On Other Methods of Writing Secretly, Which Are Contained Above.

In the preceding chapter of this first book, Most Serene Prince, forty methods of our art of Steganography were arranged in order. Although their abundance can suffice by itself for writing anything whatever secretly, nevertheless, in order that we may show students the way of [unclear] greater things, I think it worthwhile also to explain other little methods of writing by example. Therefore, just as in the preceding chapter, among the other twenty-two methods, we set down the last by transposition of the letters of the alphabet into the following ones in order, so now, according to one alphabet of twenty-two letters, necessary to us alone, let us, in each individual method, anticipate the significant letters into the preceding one. In this anticipation the first method of this chapter will agree with the last of the preceding chapter, the second with the penultimate, and so consequently down to the last of this chapter, which will be the first of the chapter, varying the method of the corresponding transposition.

The First Method of This Second Chapter Uses Individual Significant Letters, and Each Letter Is to Be Taken in One [word].

The first method of this second [chapter] uses individual significant words, and the first letter of any word whatsoever is immediately transferred into the preceding one. Thus this preceding first one is to be taken. But you must draw the alphabet in a circle, both in this method and in all the following ones in which letters are transposed, so that here z is taken for A, a for b, b for c, as is clear in the alphabet by the circle.

This method, however, like all the rest, can be varied in many ways: by alternate, double, triple, quadruple, or more [letters], at the writer’s pleasure, yet in such a way that suitable signs [are assigned] to each one; otherwise even he himself can easily forget what he has written, and no one will perceive his intention. Now, however, with the letters placed beneath, mark how much each letter is away, h2, which is the first in the alphabet of all languages; but now let us proceed to explain this method, with rather shorter sentences, as we seem to have used above.

Alphabet.

A z. b a c b d c e d f e g f h g i h k l k m l n m o n p o q p r q s t r s t u s y s x z x.

Intention of the Secret.

Wait for me tomorrow at nine with force.

Significant Letters.

Time passes. Z: i. d. t. z, q. s. i. l. h. m. d. n. q. w. l. t. la. mtm. l. b. s di s. z. k. s. i. follows.

Example of the First.

Time passes; let us strive for [zeal?], sincerely choosing light things humbly with our minds, gathering our daily errors. The time for gathering is at hand; let us cleanse the shadows of impulses, let us leave this age, fleeing the torpor of sloth; let us hold fast the zeal of Catholic holiness. Amen. Johannes Trithemius, abbot, wrote this on the sixth day before the Kalends of March, in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1500.

The Second Method Uses Alternate Words, and the Letters of the Significant Words Are Transferred into the Second Preceding One.

The second method of this chapter, beginning with one vacant word, uses alternate words, the idle and the significant being set forth in the order of the narrative; and the first letter of each significant word is anticipated, transferred immediately into the second preceding one, so that x is taken for A, z for b, a for c, and so consequently, as is clear in the round table placed here, and in the plain alphabet which we have set down for the easier manner of writing. The red letters, however, are our customary alphabet, from which each of them, in this method of writing, being mystically superimposed upon the black [letter] in the round [table], is taken for the proposed narrative.

Example of the Second. Creator of the human race, God, look upon your servants. Govern them with zeal for righteousness, so that, living well, we may obtain the reward, the joy of the heavenly ones. Help us, frail and wretched human beings, and adorn us with holy morals; [unclear], we beseech you, illumine our minds with light, so that we may diligently call to mind your passion, with tears and good works. Jesus Christ, Savior, free us by the power of your shed blood. Ruler of Catholic unity, save your gravely afflicted people, whom long ago, dying on the cross, you redeemed by your most blessed shed blood. See how grievously the people is afflicted under the most cruel Turk. Free us wretches through the [love?] by which you redeemed us.

Amen. John Trithemius, Abbot, in the year of the Lord 1500.

The Third Method proceeds through individual signifying words, and the letters are transferred to the third preceding letter.

The third method of this second chapter proceeds through individual signifying words, as the first does, and the first letter of each word is transferred to the immediately third preceding letter. Thus for A, x is taken, which is third before it through z and [y?]; and so consequently, as is clear from the letters themselves and the numbers placed in the little wheel. This method can also be varied just as the others can, and not only by proceeding through individual signifying words, but also through alternate words, pairs, threes, fours, or more, at the pleasure of any writer.

The Fourth Method uses individual signifying words, but the letters are transferred to the fourth preceding letter.

The fourth method of this chapter proceeds in order through individual significations, after the fashion of the preceding one; but the letters of the hidden mystery, moved back, are transferred to the fourth immediately preceding letter, as is shown more clearly in the little wheel set below.

And so consequently, as is clear in the little wheel. This method can also be varied with the others, by alternate words, pairs, or more; but, by proceeding as it were through individual signifying words, we can conceal many manifest secrets. For the sake of brevity it has pleased us to adopt this method.

Intention of the Secret.

The parson of Bing has died on account of something; look after the parish. This is the secret intention of the following open narrative, according to this method.

Example IV.

Z. As we are about to praise the exalter of our souls, let us continually approach in divine love, desiring whatever useless slanders, empty vanities, eternal joys; behold, all things pass away except God and justice. Why do we love this life and desire to be plunged into destruction? Why do we lead ourselves away? Let us pray to Christ, the zealous guardian of devotion and of eternal love, with continual insistence. We are daily stained by grains and are driven by temptations. Most sweet Christ, grant us zeal for love of your sweetness, and let iniquity not harm our souls. Amen. Johannes Trithemius wrote this on the Kalends of March, in the year of the Lord 1500.

The fifth method uses individual signifying letters, and each letter is changed into the fifth before it.

The fifth method of this second chapter, like the preceding one, admits no empty words, but the mystery proceeds through each of the signifying words. Nor do I believe that anyone ignorant of this art can ever discover things hidden by these methods, since even for one who knows the art but is not well practiced it becomes difficult to penetrate everything. The letters hidden in all the words of the mystery run through to the fifth immediately preceding, so that for a is taken [unclear], which is in the circle of the alphabet.

The Fifth.

G. Standing by the grains of the mind, we humbly [unclear] your letters; new ones. Zealots of the Trinity, grant us honorable good zeal; evil zeal pursues, does not work. Most merciful Christ, we humbly ask, father, come to our aid. Alas, I am heavily burdened by grave diseases; O best redeemer, grant pardon to the wretched. Johannes Trithemius, abbot, set this down on the seventh day before the Kalends of March, in the year 1500.

The sixth method proceeds through all the signifying words, and each letter is placed in the sixth preceding.

The sixth method of this chapter also proceeds through all the signifying words after the fashion of the previous one, admitting no word that is wholly empty; and all the letters of the secret mystery are transposed backward, so that before A the sixth preceding in the little wheel is taken, which is r; for b, s; for c, t; for d, [unclear]; for e, x; for f, z; for g, A; and so consequently according to the order of the alphabet set down in the little wheel itself. By means of the number placed beneath the alphabet it can easily and without labor be written how far each letter stands from another, and how far it is in the order of each alphabet. Now the little wheel follows.

Example VII. The joy of temporal goods, with flattering and slippery evils, wearies Christian peace with mortal gladness and various wars. The flesh is the vanity of the age for the criminal; those who rashly hold cheap the blessedness of the future kingdom, given over to wickedness, good for nothing, [more savage?] than beasts, wretchedly do not seek the bright path of Catholic life. They swiftly flee good things; nevertheless they perceive all Christian things as false, and the devout will more swiftly hold them in the tranquility of life. The true Catholic, who will never endure changes, truly flees the gladness of the world, does nothing rashly, does not pursue gain, loves purity; you shine with nobility by virtue; mindful of future light, he esteems transitory goods as worthless. Johannes Trithemius.

Johannes Trithemius, Abbot of Sponheim

The eighth method, indeed, in this chapter, like the preceding one, makes use throughout of significant words in the narration of the mystery, and every letter in the hidden narration is transposed into the eighth preceding letter, so that for A, p is taken, which, counting backward, is eighth from that place, as is clear in the numbering wheel. For b, q is taken; for c, r; and so on in order through the whole alphabet. This method too is varied at the pleasure of anyone who knows the art, through alternate [words?], pairs, threes, fours, or more, as we shall say in its place.

Example VIII.

Savior of souls, eternal power of the Most High Father, hear the sorrows of the wretched; he mitigates the tribulation of the innocent. Succor those laboring under temptations, poverty, and the desolation of the frail. Jesus will extend your hand of defense, so that we may deserve to be cleansed, zealots of your justice. Most kindly Son of God, drive away the darkness of sins; sweet light of souls, at all times drive away rash zeal. Glorifier of those who are zealous for your justice, help those awaiting health from you; powerfully [unclear] of the persecuting [unclear], and we are [unclear], and the most holy ray of love: grant yourself to those entreating with zeal. O most gentle Jesus, lover of uprightness, examine the tears of your zealots. In the year of the Lord M.I.D., on the Kalends of March.

The ninth method uses all signifying words, and every letter is transferred to the ninth preceding one.

Alpha

The ninth method of this preceding chapter, in concealing the proposed mystery, directs the arrangement or order through all the signifying words, and admits absolutely no empty word. But all letters in the secret narration are transferred to the ninth preceding letter, so that for d one takes o, which is ninth in the order of the alphabet before it, as appears plainly both in the wheel and in the alphabet. For b one takes p; for e, q; and so following. This method, like all the others, can be varied into many others, not only by alternate words, pairs, or triplets, but also by other arrangements so diverse that infinite methods can be made from any one method.

Of Johannes Trithemius, Abbot of Sponheim

Example IX.

Zealot of religion, Savior Jesus, most gentle of all, receive those invoking you; [unclear] free the weak and humble servants; pardon the suppliants their crimes; make blessed [unclear] calm disturbances; grant true humility to those zealous for the Lord’s salvation.

We seek more readily the zeal and justice, eternal light of the blessed; may you deign to be present to those seeking, and grant the zeal of Catholic liberty to those supplicating; and the plots of [unclear], and whatever tares trouble the sails of Christianity: holy giver of light, discern the girdle of innocence, and gird on the holy bond of Christian justice for supplicating Christians. Redeem the zeal, as we are humble ones seeing Christ in you. In the year M.I.D.7, on the Kalends of March, Johannes Trithemius, Abbot of Sponheim.

The tenth method uses individual signifying words, and every letter is transferred to the tenth preceding one.

The tenth method of this chapter, in the manner of the preceding ones, uses individual signifying words in concealing the mystery, while no word at all is mixed in. But since it would be difficult, for the concealment of the intention or the congruity of the speech, to compose by individual words, you will be able, both in this and in almost all the other methods, to use alternate words, pairs, triplets, quadruplets, or even more. But since all letters are signifying, after the pattern of the preceding methods, in this tenth method they are taken by anticipation into the tenth preceding letter, so that for A one takes n, because in the order of the alphabet, according to the demonstration of the wheel, it is ten places before it; for b one takes o; for c, p; for d, q; and so consequently through the whole alphabet, as is clear to one looking at the middle circumference.

The eleventh method, like the preceding one, uses single signifying [items], and the letters are advanced by eleven.

Threefold General Key to the Steganographic Books of Johannes Trithemius, Abbot of Sponheim: written by the author himself, and to be communicated to lovers of this art who will show gratitude and keep it secret.

At Darmstadt. Printed by Balthasar Hofmann, at the expense of Johannes Berner, bookseller of Frankfurt, in the year 1608. With privilege and the consent of superiors.

[unclear]

Threefold General Key to the Steganographic Books of Johannes Trithemius, Abbot of Sponheim.

The general keys of our book, and the principal ones, are three; on them depends the variation of all the rest. And it consists in the permutation of vowels with consonants, as you will see in the following examples:

ab {a h} ek {ap} id [unclear] eq {ir} of {om} un {os ut} ug {u n}

This method of writing must evidently be understood as follows: where, in your secret sense, the vowel a happens to have to be written by you, you should put in place of a the consonant b, and conversely, if b happens to have to be written, you should write in place of b the vowel a; thus in the remaining modes also, which are for variation, namely for ag, for ef, for id, which, just as it is the middle one, so always remains fixed and will never be changed.

{a g} {a n} {a t} {c f} {e m} {e s} {i d} [unclear] {l i r} {o c} {o k} {u p} ub)

Now, by way of example, if the word Omnipotens is to be written, it is written in this way by the first mode: Fmndpftens; by the second, Moulpmkus; but by the third mode, thus: Smnrasuqno. Conversely, namely by the three later modes: by the first thus, Cmndptfns; by the second thus, Qmnruqasne. And thus we proceed in complete sentences.

Now from these six aforesaid modes the following rules are set up, according to which you will regulate yourself in reading our book. Any one of the following modes is varied by any one of the aforesaid rules. And you will observe their variation in many parts of our book, namely in the conjurations of demons, in which our secrets are hidden, and revealed by our rules to those who know the seals.

And, as an example for you, let the following sentence serve: just as it can be written by all the aforesaid rules, so it has pleased us to put it here by the first mode. “Have mercy, almighty God, on the souls of your servants, resting piously in you.” This sentence by the first becomes thus:

Mdscrec fmndpftens icgs bndmbags obmglfrgm tgfrgm dn te pdc reqgdesecntdgm

And since, because of the lack of vowels, no word signifying anything is given to you here for mixing into our book, among so many consonants we have followed above this rule of the example, namely by taking the aforesaid consonants:

Midosa coracir ocafati co iu sa

Of these letters only the first or initial one is significant for you; immediately after it follows one that is not significant, or is vacant, and so alternately, as the points marked above over the significant letters show you. The General Key of Steganography

The sign 0, or the arithmetical [unclear], as often as it is set down, will indicate to you that many significant letters, and the number immediately following will signify that many significant letters.

The first mode is indicated thus: 10 10 10 10 10 10 10 10 etc. 01 01 01 01 01 01 01 etc. The second mode thus: 200 200 200 200 200 200 etc. The third thus: 001 001 001 001 001 001 etc. The fourth mode thus: 0001 0001 0001 0001 0001 0001 etc. The fifth mode thus: 1000 1000 1000 1000 1000 1000 etc. The sixth mode: 10000 10000 100 The eighth mode thus: 20000 20000 20

The second general key is one that is made in this way, namely that the writer goes before and the reader follows, as in this example: “Have mercy, almighty God, on the souls of your servants,” etc.; that is: lhrdqdqđ nlmbrpsdmr edtr zmhlzatr ezlknqlstnqtl, etc. Since these letters, joined in this way, would signify nothing, so likewise through the preceding eight examples or modes, as is contained in our book.

The third and last general key is made thus: if you wished to write, “Have mercy, God,” etc., as above, you will do as follows: you will count all the letters of your meaning, and, however many there are, into that many parts you will divide them; for example, if you wish to divide two by three, for one part of the whole sentence set above you will have 45 letters. Once divided, 22 will come to one part; one remains, which you will always attach at the end to the rest. You will write them in the similar way indicated below; afterwards you will vary them by the rules stated above.

Mainsiemraebuers osmanmiuplotreuns iducourfu. And this verse is divided by two; by 3, however, it is made thus: Mefinaffme dnrcleuors reau onmitmnu raopbrouutsm. By 4, however, thus: Mi auipnlfoio et mr reanenbmrs ut edfu oesu muar nsmu. And thus by dividing we proceed up to eight parts; afterwards, for making the letters signify something to the reader, with other vowels inserted, you will have this by the preceding eight rules, proceeding in our book, except that you examine each conjuration at the beginning through each of our [unclear], which will soon be clear to your industry with this key. Therefore we ask that, for the salvation of our soul, you be willing to say the Lord’s Prayer.

End.
